The view from an eleventh-floor window of an old downtown Pittsburgh office building on a rainy late-October afternoon in 2018, looking south over the Monongahela River: the river the color of slate far below, a towboat pushing a line of open coal barges downstream toward the Point, the Smithfield Street Bridge's steel lenticular trusses to the left, the steep wooded slope of Mount Washington across the river with houses along its crest, rain streaking the gray sky and hazing the far bank. Rooftops of older stone and brick buildings in the near foreground below the window. Eye level about 5 and a half feet, looking slightly down.
Smooth old plaster wall in a 1920s office building, repainted in 2018 a muted sage gray in flat paint, a few faint hairline cracks and gentle unevenness from age, no pattern.
Narrow 2 and a quarter inch oak strip flooring from the 1920s, refinished a warm honey brown, boards running top to bottom with staggered end joints, light scuffs and a slightly worn satin finish.
Smooth white painted plaster ceiling in an old office building, faintly uneven, a few fine old cracks, no fixtures.

A tall 1920s office baseboard of dark-stained oak about 8 inches high: a flat board with a small rounded cap molding along the top edge and a quarter-round shoe at the bottom, old varnish worn at the high points.
A simple 1920s dark-stained oak picture rail and crown molding about 4 inches high: a flat band with a rounded lip at the bottom for picture hooks and a small cove above, old varnish.

A 1920s-style schoolhouse pendant light seen from directly below, switched off: a round white opal milk-glass globe about 14 inches across held in a brass fitter, a short brass stem above it, the glass plain white.

A tall 1920s wooden double-hung office window with a single large pane in each sash, the wood painted dark green and chipped at the corners, brass sash locks, a deep wooden sill. Rain drops on the outside of the glass. Every pane of glass is completely transparent.
A cast-iron column radiator from the 1920s, about 4 feet wide and 2 feet tall, painted silver-gray, with its pipe connections at the bottom ends and a small round valve handle on the right.

A large bare cork bulletin board in a plain oak frame, about 7 feet wide and 4 and a half feet tall, the cork a warm tan with faint old pin holes, a small dish of red push pins and a coil of red string clipped to the bottom edge of the frame, otherwise empty.

A large framed street map of a small river town, about 5 feet wide and 3 and a half feet tall, in a thin black frame behind glass: cream paper, ochre streets, sage green parkland and a broad pale blue river curving down the right side, faint fold creases. No words, letters, numbers or street names anywhere on the map.

A 1920s oak office door, varnished honey brown and worn around the knob, with one flat panel in its lower half and a large panel of frosted glass in its upper half, the frosted glass a flat milky pale gray that nothing can be seen through, with no lettering on it. A round brass knob on the left side and a brass key plate below it, three brass hinges on the right edge.
A single brass wall coat hook with two arms on a small oak backplate, a tan trench coat hanging from it, damp at the hem.

A broad 1940s oak double-pedestal office desk, 6 feet wide, 3 feet deep and 2 feet 6 inches tall, honey-brown varnish worn pale at the front edge, three drawers in each pedestal with small brass pulls, a flat clear top, the knee space on the front side.
A 2010s black mesh-back office swivel chair with padded black seat, fixed armrests, a five-star black base on casters, about 2 feet wide and 3 feet 4 inches tall.
A wooden office side chair from the 1940s, oak with a curved back rail, a padded seat in worn oxblood leather with brass nailheads, about 1 foot 9 inches wide and 2 feet 10 inches tall.
A black 2010s office desk telephone with a small gray monochrome screen, a grid of buttons, a curved handset in its cradle and a coiled black cord, about 9 inches wide and 8 inches deep.
A closed black hardcover pocket notebook about 3 and a half by 5 and a half inches, an elastic band around it and a black ballpoint pen clipped to its cover.

A thick closed manila police case folder about 9 by 12 inches and 2 inches thick, its tab label reading exactly "18-09-1147", the corners of a few glossy photographs sticking out of one side, a rubber band around it.
A plain buff file folder about 9 by 12 inches lying closed, a white typed label on the front reading exactly "FINAL REPORT".
A closed slate blue county laboratory folder about 9 by 12 inches, a white label on the front reading exactly "LAB REPORT".
An open silver 2017 laptop computer with a 15-inch screen, a black keyboard, the screen dark, about 14 inches wide and 10 inches deep.
A black wire mesh desk letter tray about 10 by 13 inches and 3 inches tall holding a few loose printed laboratory report pages with soft, unreadable text.
A brass banker's desk lamp with a green glass shade, 15 inches tall, a small pull chain, switched off.

A four-drawer vertical steel filing cabinet from the 1980s, painted putty beige with chips at the edges, chrome drawer handles and small label holders with blank cards, 15 inches wide, 2 feet 4 inches deep and 4 feet 4 inches tall.
A plain oak bookcase from the 1950s, 3 feet wide, 1 foot deep and 6 feet tall, five shelves holding law books with plain cloth spines, binders and a few file boxes, nothing readable on the spines.

Wet, worn residential asphalt road surface: dark charcoal gray with fine gravel aggregate showing through, a few thin sealed cracks, damp patches darker than the rest, scattered small fallen yellow and brown maple and oak leaves.
A small front lawn in late October: cool-season grass gone a little long and wet, matted in places, scattered fallen brown oak leaves and yellow maple leaves.
An old concrete sidewalk of square slabs, each slab 5 feet across, pale gray concrete darkened by rain, hairline cracks, one slightly heaved edge, a few wet fallen leaves stuck to it.

Looking straight down at two faint parallel black tire skid marks on asphalt, about 50 feet long, mostly washed away by six weeks of rain, broken and patchy. They run straight from the right edge, then swing in a long gentle curve up toward the top left corner. Only the marks; everything else is transparent.

Looking straight down at a scatter of small crumbs of broken tempered car window glass, cube-shaped pieces a quarter inch across, pale green-white, in a loose drift about 5 feet long along a road gutter, a few wet leaves among them. Only the glass and leaves; everything else is transparent.

The north side of a residential street in a small western Pennsylvania steel town on a gray, wet late-October afternoon in 2018, seen from across the street: a row of two-story red and brown brick houses from the 1920s with deep front porches, steep concrete steps and small front lawns, the house straight ahead (412) with a white porch and a green door, bare and half-bare maple trees with yellow leaves, wooden utility poles with sagging wires, and above the rooftops the faint smokestacks of an old steel mill against a low, clouded slate gray sky. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

The south side of a residential street in a small western Pennsylvania steel town on a gray, wet late-October afternoon in 2018: a row of two-story brick houses from the 1920s with porches and steep front steps, small wet front lawns, a gravel driveway between two houses, a tall dark green privet hedge along the front of the house on the left, bare maple branches, wooden utility poles with wires and a low, clouded slate gray sky. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

The front of a two-story red brick house from the 1920s seen straight on, about 20 feet wide: two double-hung windows with white trim on the upper floor; on the ground floor, raised about 4 feet above the ground, a front door with a white frame near the right end and a wide front window to its left; a dark gray shingle hip roof with one small dormer, a black metal house number plaque beside the door that reads exactly "409", a black metal mailbox on the wall. The front door is a dark green six-panel door. Nothing in front of the house; the porch is separate.
A dark green painted six-panel wooden front door from the 1920s, no window, a brass knob and brass deadbolt on the right side, a brass kick plate at the bottom, in a white painted wooden door frame.

Looking west down a straight residential street of 1920s brick houses with porches on both sides in a small western Pennsylvania steel town on a gray, wet late-October afternoon in 2018: parked cars from the 2010s along both curbs, maple and oak trees in yellow and brown, wooden utility poles and wires, at the far end of the block a cross street with a low brick corner store, the hills beyond hazy under a low slate gray sky. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

Looking east along a residential street in a small western Pennsylvania steel town on a gray, wet late-October afternoon in 2018, where the road bends to the right and out of sight behind a tall, thick dark green privet hedge about 9 feet high on the right; on the left the last brick houses of the block and a big oak, wet asphalt curving away, a wooden utility pole at the bend, low slate gray clouds. Nothing of the road can be seen past the bend. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

A large mature northern red oak street tree, about 50 feet tall with a broad crown about 36 feet across, a thick straight gray-brown trunk about 3 feet in diameter with deeply ridged bark, leaves turned rust brown and partly fallen. On one side of the trunk at bumper height, 1 to 2 feet off the ground, a pale gash in the bark about 2 feet long where fresh bark has started to grow over the wound. Roots spreading into a small patch of grass.

A small roadside memorial at the foot of a tree, about 3 feet wide and 1 foot 2 inches tall: six glass jar candles with burned-down wax, a laminated color snapshot of a smiling young woman and man propped on a small wooden stake, a few wilted bunches of grocery store flowers in cellophane, and a rain-soaked gray stuffed rabbit sitting in front.

A low, overgrown yew hedge along the front of a small yard, about 7 feet long, 2 and a half feet deep and 4 feet tall, dark green and untrimmed, its woody roots and the base thick with six weeks of fallen brown oak leaves.

A wooden utility pole about 28 feet tall, weathered gray, with a 2010s cobra-head streetlight on a curved aluminum arm near the top, a few insulators and a short length of cut wire at the crossarm, a small metal pole tag.

The front porch and steps of a 1920s red brick house, 20 feet wide and 8 feet deep, the porch floor 4 feet above the ground on a red brick base, gray painted wooden floorboards, four square white wooden columns holding a low hip roof with dark gray shingles about 12 feet high, white wooden railings with square balusters, and a run of six steep concrete steps 4 feet wide coming down the front toward the street near the right end of the porch as seen from the street, with a black iron handrail. A porch light fixture beside where the door would be. Total depth with steps 12 feet.

A tall, thick privet hedge along the front of a yard, 30 feet long, 3 and a half feet deep and 9 feet tall, dense dark green small leaves with a few yellowing, trimmed flat on top and the front face, solid enough that nothing can be seen through it.
A 2013 midsize four-door sedan in dull dark red, ordinary and a little dusty, wet with rain, nothing on the plates readable, 6 feet wide, 15 and a half feet long and 4 feet 10 inches tall.

The view from the front window of a 1920s brick house on Alder Street in a small western Pennsylvania steel town on a gray late-October afternoon in 2018: the house's own front porch railing in the near foreground, a small wet lawn, the street, and directly across it a large oak at the curb with a small memorial of glass jar candles and flowers at its foot, brick houses with porches behind it. At the right edge, a tall dark green privet hedge blocks the view down the street. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

The view from the front window of a 1920s brick house on Alder Street in a small western Pennsylvania steel town at about eight on a rainy late-October night in 2018: the porch railing in the near foreground, the wet lawn, the empty wet street, and across it a large dark oak at the curb with small glass jar candles at its foot. At the left edge, the rain-wet hood of a dark green early-2010s station wagon parked in the driveway. At the right edge, a tall dark privet hedge. Dark blue-black sky, nobody in sight. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

The view from a kitchen window at the back of a 1920s brick house in a small western Pennsylvania steel town on a gray late-October afternoon in 2018: a narrow backyard with a wet lawn and fallen leaves, a vegetable bed cut back for winter, a wooden picnic table, a chain-link fence, a detached one-car garage with a shingled roof, the backs of the houses on the next street, a low slate gray sky. Eye level about 5 and a half feet, a little above the sink.

The view from a kitchen window at the back of a 1920s brick house at about eight on a rainy late-October night in 2018: the dark shape of a narrow backyard, a wooden picnic table and a chain-link fence barely made out, the dark outline of a detached garage, the backs of the houses on the next street with a few windows, a dark sky. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

The view out through a front door standing partly open, at about eight on a rainy late-October night in 2018: a gray painted wooden porch floor wet at the edge, a white porch column and railing, the porch light fixture on the wall beside the door, steep concrete steps going down to a wet lawn and an empty wet street, a large dark oak across the street. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.
Smooth old plaster wall in a 1920s house, painted a warm cream in eggshell paint, softly uneven with faint brush texture, no pattern.

Original 1920s red oak strip flooring, 2 and a quarter inch boards running top to bottom with staggered joints, a medium amber varnish worn lighter in traffic areas, small dents and scratches of a lived-in home.
Smooth painted plaster ceiling in an older house, flat white, faintly uneven, no fixtures.
A 1920s house baseboard about 7 inches high, painted white in semi-gloss: a flat board with a simple ogee cap along the top and a small quarter-round shoe at the bottom, a few scuffs.
A plain 1920s painted white picture rail about 2 inches high: a flat band with a small rounded lip at the bottom edge.
A flush ceiling light seen from directly below, switched off: a round frosted white glass dome about 13 inches across with a small brushed nickel finial in the middle.
A small five-arm brass dining room chandelier from the 1990s seen from directly below, switched off: curved brass arms each with a small white frosted glass shade, a round brass center column.

A dark green painted six-panel wooden front door from the 1920s seen from inside the house, closed, no window, a brass knob and brass deadbolt on the left side, three brass hinges on the right edge, in a white painted wooden door frame with plain casing.

A white painted wooden front door frame with plain casing seen straight on from inside a house, the dark green six-panel door swung inward and standing open about a foot, its brass knob on the left edge of the door. On the left jamb at shoulder height, about 5 feet up, a dark reddish-brown smear about four inches long. The gap of the open doorway, between the door edge and the frame, is completely transparent.
A small wall-mounted wooden key rack painted white with four brass hooks, a ring of car and house keys hanging from one hook.

A wide wooden double-hung window from the 1920s with a single pane in each sash, painted white, a wide flat sill, sheer white curtains pushed back to both sides on a plain rod. Every pane of glass is completely transparent.

A staggered group of eight framed photographs hung in a rising diagonal, stepping up from right to left as if following a staircase, in matching thin black frames with white mats: high school staff group photos with rows of people in front of brick school buildings, and one of a bearded man in a hard hat standing beside a surveyor's tripod in a field, squinting. Faces small and soft, no readable writing.

A wooden double-hung kitchen window from the 1920s, painted white, a single pane in each sash, a short pale yellow cafe curtain on a brass rod across the lower half. Every pane of glass is completely transparent.
A painted cream wooden kitchen wall cabinet with two flat-panel doors and small brass knobs, about 2 and a half feet wide and 2 and a half feet tall, seen straight on.

A white painted wooden back door with a window of nine small panes in its upper half, a gathered white cotton curtain covering the whole window on the inside so nothing shows through, a brass knob and deadbolt on the right side.

Looking straight down at a long hall runner rug, 3 feet wide and 11 feet long, a traditional Persian-style pattern in deep red, navy and cream with a darker border and a short fringe at both ends, a little worn in the middle.
A narrow cherry wood hall table, 3 feet wide, 1 foot 2 inches deep and 2 feet 7 inches tall, one shallow drawer with a brass knob, tapered legs, a small ceramic dish for mail on top.
A table lamp with a round glazed ceramic base in sage green, about 2 feet tall with its shade, a pleated off-white fabric drum shade, switched off.

The same table lamp lying on its side on the floor: a round glazed sage green ceramic base about 2 feet long lying sideways, its pleated off-white fabric drum shade crushed flat and bent on one side, the cord trailing.

A pair of women's reading glasses with thin tortoiseshell frames lying on the floor, one temple arm bent backward, a thin beaded eyeglass chain of small amber and gold beads still attached, about 5 and a half inches wide.
A low two-tier wooden shoe rack, 2 feet 5 inches wide, 1 foot deep and 1 foot 6 inches tall, holding a pair of men's brown work boots, women's black flats and a pair of sneakers.

A straight 1920s interior staircase against a wall, 3 and a half feet wide, rising 9 feet over 12 feet of run in fourteen steps, oak treads with a worn varnish and white painted risers, a white painted square newel post at the bottom and a dark stained oak handrail on white balusters along the open side.
A low cherry wood TV cabinet from the 2000s, 5 feet wide, 1 foot 7 inches deep and 2 feet tall, two cabinet doors and an open middle shelf with a cable box.
A 2016 flat-screen television, 50 inches, thin black bezel on a black center stand, the screen dark, 3 feet 8 inches wide and 2 feet 3 inches tall on its stand.
A three-seat sofa from the 2000s upholstered in oatmeal tweed fabric, rolled arms, loose back cushions, a folded plum knit throw over one arm, 7 feet long, 3 feet deep and 2 feet 10 inches tall.
A rectangular cherry wood coffee table, 4 feet long, 2 feet wide and 1 foot 6 inches tall, a lower shelf with a stack of magazines and a small bowl of reading glasses cases.
A comfortable wingback armchair in faded navy and cream plaid upholstery, about 2 feet 9 inches wide and 3 feet 6 inches tall, a small embroidered cushion.
A brushed brass floor lamp about 5 feet tall with a simple round base and a white linen drum shade, switched off.
A rectangular cherry wood dining table from the 1990s, 6 feet long, 3 and a half feet wide and 2 feet 6 inches tall, turned legs, a cream table runner down the middle.
A cherry wood dining chair with a ladder back of three curved slats and a cream fabric seat cushion, 1 foot 6 inches wide and 3 feet 2 inches tall.
A closed gray school-issue laptop computer from about 2017, plain plastic case with a small asset sticker on the lid, 13 inches wide and 9 inches deep.
An open gray school-issue laptop computer from about 2017, plain plastic case, the screen up and dark, 13 inches wide and 9 inches deep.

A 2000s white top-freezer refrigerator, 2 feet 11 inches wide, 2 feet 9 inches deep and 5 feet 9 inches tall, with a paper wall calendar held to the lower door by magnets: a school district calendar turned to October with a photo of a high school marching band at the top and soft, unreadable handwriting in some date squares. A few photo magnets and a child's drawing beside it.

A run of 1990s kitchen base cabinets 8 feet long, 2 feet deep and 3 feet tall, painted cream with small brass knobs, a speckled tan laminate countertop and a white double-bowl sink set into the middle with a chrome gooseneck faucet, a dish rack beside it.

A white 2000s freestanding electric range with four coil burners, a back control panel with knobs, an oven door with a window and a long handle, 2 feet 6 inches wide, 2 feet 3 inches deep and 3 feet tall to the cooktop.
A wide shallow blue-glazed ceramic bowl about 1 foot across holding a pile of red and yellow apples.
A small square painted wooden kitchen table, white legs and a natural maple top, 3 feet square and 2 feet 6 inches tall.
A neat stack of high school student papers about 3 inches tall, a red pen lying on top, soft unreadable handwriting on the top sheet.

A black and white marbled composition notebook lying open, its pages filled with neat soft unreadable handwriting, a blue ballpoint pen lying in the fold, about 15 inches wide open and 10 inches tall.
A plain white ceramic mug of cold tea with a paper tea bag tag hanging over its rim, 4 inches tall.

The view from a second-floor police station window through half-open horizontal blinds on a gray late-October afternoon in 2018: a fenced impound lot of cracked asphalt below, a few towed cars, and in the middle a silver 2010s compact SUV parked with its left side toward the window, partly covered by a blue plastic tarp tied down at the front, its left rear quarter panel uncovered and showing a long dent, its windows shot out. Chain-link fence with barbed wire, a brick municipal garage beyond, low gray sky. Eye level about 5 and a half feet, looking down a little.

Painted concrete block wall in a 1970s municipal building, blocks 16 by 8 inches in a running bond, painted pale gray-blue in semi-gloss, the mortar joints slightly recessed, a few chips and old patched anchor holes.
Vinyl composition floor tiles 12 inches square, a light gray with fine darker gray and white flecks, laid in a grid with faint seams, a few scuffs and a dull worn wax finish.

A suspended acoustic drop ceiling of 2 by 2 foot white mineral fiber tiles with a fine pinhole fissured texture in a thin white metal grid, one tile slightly water-stained at a corner, no fixtures or vents.
A 4-inch black rubber cove wall base, matte, with a small rounded toe at the bottom, a few scuffs.

A 2 by 4 foot recessed fluorescent troffer light seen from directly below, switched off: a white metal frame with a flat prismatic acrylic lens showing a fine square pattern, the tubes faint behind it.

A wide aluminum-framed office window from the 1970s, about 8 feet wide and 4 and a half feet tall, two fixed panes, beige horizontal mini blinds raised halfway with their slats tilted open. Every pane of glass and the gaps between the slats are completely transparent.

A police detective's cork case board in an aluminum frame, about 8 feet wide and 4 and a half feet tall, covered with pinned color photographs of a crashed silver compact SUV against a tree, a printed street map with two red X's drawn on it, a printed gas station receipt, index cards and a yellow sticky note in neat handwriting that reads exactly "Why leave the wallets?". All other writing soft and unreadable.

A second police cork case board in an aluminum frame, about 8 feet wide and 4 and a half feet tall: a printout of a brick house's front with the number "409" readable, a printed map of a riverside road, two school staff head-and-shoulders photos of a Black woman and a bearded white man, index cards with soft unreadable writing, and a line of red marker drawn from the left edge of the board across to a pinned photo.

A steel interior door painted gray-blue with a narrow vertical window of wired safety glass in its upper half, a black plastic sign above the window that reads exactly "INTERVIEW 1", a brushed steel lever handle on the right side and a steel kick plate. The wired glass is completely transparent apart from its fine wire grid.
A solid steel corridor door painted gray-blue, no window, a brushed steel lever handle on the left side, a steel kick plate at the bottom and a door closer at the top, in a steel frame.

A 1960s wooden library chair in light oak with a curved back rail and spindles, about 1 foot 7 inches wide and 2 feet 10 inches tall.

An old oak service counter from the 1910s, 8 feet long, 2 and a half feet deep and 3 feet 6 inches tall, the public side faced in raised panels, the top worn smooth, a brass bell and a cup of pens on top.

A large open hardbound visitor sign-in ledger lying flat, about 2 feet wide open and 15 inches tall, ruled pages with columns of soft unreadable handwritten names and times, a ballpoint pen on a chain.
A long 1910s oak library table, 10 feet long, 3 and a half feet wide and 2 feet 6 inches tall, thick turned legs and a dark amber varnished top worn pale at the edges.

A white cardboard records storage box with a lift-off lid, 15 inches long, 12 inches wide and 10 inches tall, the lid set beside it, a printed label on the end that reads exactly "RD-2018-044", stuffed with paper files in manila folders.

A wide steel flat-file map cabinet from the 1970s painted olive gray, 4 feet 6 inches wide, 3 feet 6 inches deep and 3 feet 4 inches tall, ten shallow wide drawers with long chrome pulls and small card holders, one drawer pulled open a few inches.
A run of gray steel archive shelving, 8 feet long, 2 feet deep and 7 feet 6 inches tall, six shelves packed with white cardboard records boxes with soft unreadable labels on their ends.
Painted concrete block basement wall, 16 by 8 inch blocks in running bond, painted a pale cream in thick old enamel, a few faint efflorescence stains and chips, no pattern.
An old basement concrete floor painted battleship gray, the paint worn through to bare concrete in patches, a few hairline cracks.
A rough board-formed concrete ceiling painted off-white, the faint grain of the old wooden forms showing in long parallel strips, no fixtures or pipes.
A basement ceiling light seen from directly below, switched off: a clear glass jelly-jar globe over a bulb inside a round black steel wire cage on a porcelain base.
An open doorway in a cream painted block wall, about 4 feet wide and 7 and a half feet tall, in a plain gray-painted steel frame with no door. The opening itself is completely transparent.
A gray steel electrical panel box on a basement wall, about 1 and a half feet wide and 2 and a half feet tall, its door closed, a few conduit pipes running up out of its top.

A plain steel-legged work table from the 1970s with a scratched brown laminate top, 6 feet long, 3 feet wide and 2 feet 6 inches tall, a few records boxes with lids off and a loose stack of yellowed files on it.
A white plastic basement dehumidifier on casters, 1 foot 3 inches wide, 11 inches deep and 2 feet tall, a small control panel on top, switched off.
A wet gravel access road surface of crushed gray stone and packed dirt, shallow muddy puddles, tire ruts, a few weeds and bits of rusty scrap pushed into the gravel.
An overgrown vacant industrial field in late October: tangled dead brown and tan weeds, goldenrod gone to seed, flattened wet grass, patches of gravel and broken concrete showing through.

The view to the end of a dead-end gravel road in an old riverfront industrial district of a western Pennsylvania steel town on an overcast late-October morning in 2018 after rain: a strip of weeds and riprap, then the wide slate gray river, a coal barge moored at the far bank, the steel truss bridge downstream on the left, the far bank's wooded hills in rust and gold with a few houses, low gray clouds. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

The view toward a scrapyard beside a gravel road in an old riverfront industrial district on an overcast late-October morning in 2018 after rain: a tall chain-link fence with privacy slats and coils of barbed wire, heaps of rusted scrap metal, crushed cars and old appliances behind it, a yellow material-handling crane with a grapple, a corrugated steel shed, low gray clouds. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

The view across a weedy field to a riverfront construction site on an overcast late-October morning in 2018 after rain: orange plastic construction fencing on steel posts, the cracked concrete slab and low broken brick walls of a demolished old plating works, piles of gravel and stacked pipe, a parked yellow excavator, the gray river beyond, low gray clouds. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

Looking back down a long, straight gravel access road through weeds and scrub toward a paved two-lane river road a quarter mile away, on an overcast late-October morning in 2018 after rain: puddles in the ruts, a row of wooden utility poles with sagging wires, the scrapyard's chain-link fence along the left side, a parked police patrol car halfway down, rusting old mill buildings and wooded hills on the horizon. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

A dark gray (Ford Magnetic metallic) 2016 Ford Explorer full-size SUV after a partial fire: the rear passenger windows blackened with soot and cracked, soot streaks up the rear pillars and roof, the paint blistered around the rear doors, the front half undamaged, a black roof rack, a small amber strobe light on the left of the dashboard, the right front wheel-arch trim newer and blacker than the other three. On the rear hatch, smoke-stained white vinyl capital lettering on two lines that reads exactly "BELL SECURITY" over "UNIT 4". Wet with rain, mud on the tires. 6 feet 7 inches wide, 16 feet 7 inches long and 5 feet 10 inches tall.

A square of yellow police barrier tape strung at waist height between six orange-and-white striped traffic delineator posts on rubber bases, about 22 feet wide and 30 feet long, the tape sagging and wet, printed in black capitals that read exactly "POLICE LINE DO NOT CROSS" repeating along it. The inside of the square is empty.
A red plastic 5-gallon gasoline can with a black spout, lying on its side, scuffed, 1 foot 4 inches long and 1 foot 2 inches tall.
A 40-foot straight section of an abandoned railroad siding: two rusted steel rails on weathered, cracked wooden ties half sunk in gravel ballast, weeds growing between the ties.

A rusted steel railroad bumping post at the dead end of a siding, about 9 feet wide, 3 feet deep and 4 feet tall, a heavy steel frame with a red-painted wooden beam across its face, the paint mostly flaked off.

A weathered wooden utility pole about 18 feet tall standing just inside a chain-link fence, with a white bullet-style security camera on a bracket near the top angled down toward the road, a gray junction box and conduit running down the pole.

A white modular construction site office trailer, 32 feet long, 12 feet wide and 11 feet tall including gray skirting, white ribbed aluminum siding, three small windows with blinds, a steel door near one end at the top of three metal steps, and beside the door a white rectangular sign that reads exactly "BELL SECURITY".
A green steel 6-yard front-load dumpster with two black plastic lids closed, rusted at the bottom, 6 feet wide, 5 feet 6 inches deep and 4 feet 6 inches tall.

A 2016 Ford Police Interceptor Utility patrol SUV in plain white with a single dark blue stripe along the sides, a low black light bar on the roof switched off, a push bumper on the front, no lettering, wet with rain. 6 feet 7 inches wide, 16 feet 6 inches long and 5 feet 9 inches tall.
Smooth painted drywall in a modern laboratory, a clean warm white in washable semi-gloss paint, perfectly even, no pattern.
Seamless commercial sheet vinyl lab flooring, light gray with a fine darker gray and white speckle, smooth and clean with a low sheen without reflections.
A suspended ceiling of 2 by 2 foot smooth white washable vinyl-faced lab ceiling tiles in a thin white metal grid, clean and even, no fixtures or vents.
A 4-inch light gray vinyl cove wall base, smooth and clean, with a small rounded toe at the bottom.
A 2 by 4 foot flat LED ceiling panel light seen from directly below, switched off: a thin white aluminum frame around a smooth frosted white diffuser.

A wall-mounted whiteboard in a thin aluminum frame, about 8 feet wide and 4 feet tall, a few rows of soft unreadable notes and a small diagram in blue marker, and across the top in neat black marker capitals and lowercase it reads exactly "Consistent with is not the same as matches. S.R.", a marker tray along the bottom with three markers and an eraser.

A heavy solid-core laboratory door with a light maple wood veneer, a narrow vertical window of frosted wired glass in its upper half that is a flat milky white with nothing seen through it, a brushed steel lever handle on the right side, a steel kick plate, and a small black plastic sign above the window that reads exactly "TRACE EVIDENCE".

A wall-mounted emergency eyewash station: a stainless steel bowl with two yellow spray heads and a yellow push flag, above it a bright green square sign with a white eye-and-water symbol and no words.
A round institutional wall clock about 12 inches across, a white plastic rim, a white face with black numbers 1 to 12, black hands and a red second hand.

A bank of gray steel evidence lockers, 12 feet long, 2 feet deep and 6 feet 6 inches tall: three rows of square locking doors, each with a small keypad lock and a strip of white tape with a soft handwritten case number, one strip in the middle row that reads exactly "18-09-1147" in black marker.

A long laboratory wall bench, 14 feet long, 2 feet 6 inches deep and 3 feet tall, a black epoxy resin top on white steel base cabinets with drawers and doors, a raised shelf of reagent bottles along the back edge.

A forensic comparison microscope from the 2010s: two matching microscope bodies joined by an optical bridge to one binocular eyepiece, off-white and black, a stage under each objective, about 2 feet 6 inches wide and 2 feet tall.

A neat row of eight clear plastic evidence bags lying flat side by side, each sealed with a red tamper-evident strip and a white write-on label with soft unreadable writing, holding small items: a swab tube, paint chips, a black plastic fragment, a cloth glove, about 4 feet long in all.
A compact black and gray desktop label printer, 7 inches wide, 9 inches deep and 6 inches tall, a strip of white blank labels feeding out of the front.

A laboratory fume hood, 6 feet wide, 2 feet 10 inches deep and 8 feet tall, white powder-coated steel with a black epoxy work surface, a clear vertical sliding glass sash raised partway, base cabinets underneath, a small digital airflow monitor at the side.

A laboratory sink cabinet, 6 feet long, 2 feet 2 inches deep and 3 feet tall, white steel base cabinets with a black epoxy top and a deep black epoxy sink with a tall gooseneck faucet and a paper towel dispenser.

A freestanding laboratory island bench, 10 feet long, 4 feet wide and 3 feet tall, a black epoxy top on white steel cabinets on both sides, a power and data strip along the middle, a rack of test tubes, a box of nitrile gloves and a closed laptop on top.
A laboratory stool with a round black polyurethane seat on a chrome gas lift and a five-star base on casters, a chrome foot ring, about 2 feet across and 2 feet 6 inches tall.

A 1920s cast-iron steam radiator standing on short legs, ten tall slender columns with a small scrolled pattern cast into each, painted dull silver with the paint worn through to dark iron on the top edges, a round valve handle at one end. Seen straight on, the gaps between the columns completely transparent.

A round 1920s schoolhouse wall clock about fifteen inches across, a dark oak case with a brass bezel, a cream dial with plain black Arabic numerals 1 to 12 and black spade hands at ten past nine, a small brass pendulum window below the dial. Seen straight on.

A 1920s four-drawer oak vertical filing cabinet with a golden oak finish, slightly worn on the edges, each drawer with a brass bin pull and a small brass label holder holding a blank card. 1 foot 3 inches wide, 2 feet 2 inches deep, 4 feet 4 inches tall. Upright, all drawers closed.

A 1920s black office typewriter, an Underwood-style standard machine with a black enameled frame, round glass-topped keys in four rows with white rims, a chrome carriage return lever, a black platen roller and thin gold pinstripes, no brand name or lettering. 1 foot 2 inches wide, 1 foot 1 inch deep, 10 inches tall. Upright, a blank sheet of paper in the roller.

A black 1920s candlestick telephone: a tall slim black enameled stand on a round weighted base, a trumpet-shaped mouthpiece at the top, and a black cone earpiece hanging on the hook at the side on a cloth-covered cord. 5 inches across the base, 12 inches tall. Upright, earpiece on the hook.

A plain cream business envelope from the 1920s, about 9 and a half by 4 inches, sealed, lying flat, slightly creased at one corner, completely blank with no writing, stamp or lettering. About a quarter inch thick.

A plain 1910s oak side chair with a slatted back of three vertical spindles, a curved top rail, a solid saddle seat, turned legs with a stretcher between them, a golden oak finish worn pale on the seat front. 1 foot 5 inches wide, 1 foot 6 inches deep, 3 feet tall. Upright, facing forward.

Upper office wall of a 1910s Loop office building: smooth painted plaster in a warm tan, slightly aged and faintly mottled with fine hairline cracks, no pattern, the brushwork of the paint just visible at a scale of a few inches.

Lower office wall wainscot of a 1910s Loop office building: quarter-sawn golden oak paneling with a dark varnish, tall rectangular raised panels about 2 feet wide separated by plain flat stiles about 4 inches wide, the ray-fleck grain of the oak visible, worn a little paler at hip height.

A 1910s office floor of narrow oak strip boards about 2 and a quarter inches wide, laid lengthwise, honey brown under old amber varnish, scuffed into a duller gray-brown in patches, the board ends staggered, a few small dark nail holes.
A smooth cream painted plaster ceiling, aged to a faint yellow, with a few fine hairline cracks and no pattern.
A tall 1910s office baseboard of dark varnished golden oak: a plain flat board about 8 inches tall topped by a small rounded cap molding, with a narrow quarter-round shoe at the bottom.
A 1910s oak chair rail cap: a flat dark varnished golden oak band about 3 inches tall with a rounded top edge and a small bead along its bottom edge.
A simple 1910s plaster cove crown molding about 5 inches tall, painted cream, a smooth concave curve with one small flat step along its bottom edge.
A 1920s schoolhouse pendant light seen from directly below: a round white milk-glass globe about 14 inches across with a brass neck ring and a short brass stem, switched off.

A tall 1910s office window: a double-hung wooden window with a dark varnished oak frame and a wide flat casing, an upper sash and a lower sash each with one large pane, a brass sash lock where they meet, rain droplets beaded on the glass. Every glass pane is completely transparent apart from the scattered droplets.

The view from a seventh-floor office window on West Monroe Street in the Chicago Loop at nine on a wet October morning in 1927, just after the rain has stopped: across the narrow street, the soot-darkened stone and terra cotta face of a tall office building with rows of windows, the steel girders of the elevated tracks crossing at the end of the block with a train of wooden cars on them, the wet street seven floors down with black Model T Fords and a streetcar, a low pale gray overcast sky. Eye level about 5 and a half feet above the seventh floor.

A 1910s office door of dark varnished oak, a large frosted glass pane in its upper half and one flat recessed panel below, a brass knob on the left side with a brass escutcheon plate, a plain oak casing around it. On the frosted glass, in plain gold leaf block capitals outlined in black, two centered lines that read exactly "ASHBY & LOWE" and below it "DETECTIVES". The frosted glass is a soft milky translucent white, not see-through.

The view through an open office door into the seventh-floor corridor of a 1910s Chicago office building in 1927: a narrow corridor with a white and gray small hexagonal tile floor, tan plaster walls over dark oak wainscot, a row of oak office doors with frosted glass panes across the way, their lettering too far to read, and a brass mail chute on the wall. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

A large 1920s cork bulletin board about 6 feet wide and 4 feet tall in a plain dark oak frame, the brown cork surface empty apart from a few colored map pins stuck along the top edge and a small hank of red string hanging from one pin. Seen straight on.

A framed 1920s street map of Chicago about 4 feet wide and 3 feet tall in a narrow black frame behind glass: a pale cream paper map of the city street grid in fine brown lines, Lake Michigan as a pale blue band down the whole right side, the Chicago River in blue entering from the lake and forking in a Y to the west, green patches for parks, no readable words. Seen straight on.

A heavy 1910s golden oak flat-top double-pedestal office desk with a dark varnish worn pale along the front edge, three drawers in each pedestal with brass bin pulls, a center drawer, and a green felt desk blotter in a dark leather frame on top. 5 feet 6 inches wide, 3 feet deep, 2 feet 6 inches tall. Upright.

A 1920s oak swivel office chair on four legs with casters, a curved oak slatted back and arms, a saddle seat, a golden oak finish worn on the arms. 2 feet wide, 2 feet deep, 3 feet 2 inches tall. Upright, facing forward.

A 1910s oak office armchair for visitors with a plain curved back rail, flat arms and a brown leather seat held with brass tacks, a golden oak finish. 1 foot 11 inches wide, 1 foot 10 inches deep, 2 feet 10 inches tall. Upright, facing forward.

A 1920s banker's desk lamp with a solid brass base and stem and a rectangular green cased-glass shade, cream on the inside, with a small brass pull chain. 10 inches wide, 9 inches deep, 15 inches tall. Upright, switched off.
A plain 1910s oak side table with one shallow drawer with a brass knob, four square tapered legs and a dark varnished top. 3 feet wide, 1 foot 6 inches deep, 2 feet 6 inches tall. Upright.

A closed manila police case folder from 1927, about 9 by 12 inches and half an inch thick with papers inside, lying flat, a white typed label on the cover with two lines that read exactly "VALE, ARTHUR" and "27-10-2117".

A small black leather detective's notebook from the 1920s, about 4 by 6 inches, closed, with a yellow wooden pencil tucked into its spine loop, lying flat, the leather worn at the corners. About half an inch thick.
A 1920s wire desk tray of brass-plated steel wire, about 10 by 13 inches and 3 inches tall, holding a few opened cream envelopes and folded letters with no readable writing.
A closed manila report folder from the 1920s, about 9 by 12 inches and a quarter inch thick, lying flat, with a small blank white paper label on the cover and no readable words anywhere.

A large flat manila envelope from 1927, about 10 by 13 inches, sealed with a metal clasp, lying flat, stamped in red ink across the front in block capitals exactly "OFFICE OF THE CITY CHEMIST". About a quarter inch thick.
A small lavender notepaper envelope from 1927, about 6 by 4 and a half inches, sealed, lying flat, addressed in green ink handwriting that is soft and unreadable. About an eighth of an inch thick.

A 1920s office dictating machine: a black enameled cast-iron cabinet top mechanism with a horizontal brass mandrel carrying a brown wax cylinder, a small black speaking tube on a cloth hose coiled beside it, and a small open wooden box holding five more brown wax cylinders upright. 1 foot 4 inches wide, 10 inches deep, 10 inches tall. Upright.

A 1920s oak typewriter stand: a small square oak table with a lower shelf, four square legs on small casters, a dark varnish. 1 foot 8 inches wide, 1 foot 6 inches deep, 2 feet 2 inches tall. Upright.

A 1920s bentwood coat tree in dark stained beech, a tall central pole with six curled hooks at the top and a curved four-legged base, a brown felt fedora hanging on one hook. 1 foot 10 inches across the base, 6 feet 2 inches tall. Upright.

The view through an open door into the 19th-floor corridor of a Chicago radio station in October 1927: a long Art Deco corridor with a polished cream and black terrazzo floor in a stepped chevron border, pale champagne plaster walls over walnut wainscot, flat brass wall sconces switched off, a walnut studio door with a small square window across the way, its lettering too far to read. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

A radio studio wall hung from top to bottom with heavy deep oxblood red cotton velvet drapes in soft even vertical folds, each fold about 6 inches across, the pile faintly crushed and darker in the hollows, slightly dusty, no rod, no hem and no gaps.

A 1920s radio studio's wall-to-wall wool broadloom carpet in a deep bottle green with a small regular figure of tiny cream and gold diamonds about 2 inches apart, the pile flattened and a little worn in places.

A 1920s radio studio ceiling of soft off-white fiberboard acoustic panels about 2 feet square with fine perforated pinholes in a tight grid and narrow flush seams between the panels, faintly yellowed.
A plain 1920s walnut baseboard about 6 inches tall, dark satin finish, a flat face with a small rounded top edge.

A 1920s Art Deco ceiling light seen from directly below: a shallow round frosted glass bowl about 16 inches across with a stepped sunburst pattern molded in the glass, held by a flat brass ring with three small brass clips, switched off.

A 1920s Art Deco interior door of dark satin walnut with two tall flat recessed panels and a small square window of clear glass at eye height, a brass lever handle on the right side with a narrow rectangular brass backplate, a plain walnut casing. The window glass is completely transparent.
Upper wall of a 1920s Art Deco radio station office on a high floor: smooth painted plaster in a pale champagne beige with a faint soft sheen, slightly aged, no pattern.

Lower wall wainscot of a 1920s Art Deco radio station office: flat panels of book-matched walnut veneer in a warm dark brown with a satin finish, each panel about 2 feet wide, divided by thin vertical strips of black lacquered wood about half an inch wide.
A 1920s Art Deco baseboard about 6 inches tall of black lacquered wood with a thin brass strip along its top edge.
A 1920s Art Deco chair rail cap of dark satin walnut about 2 inches tall, flat-faced with a single small stepped edge on top.
A 1920s Art Deco plaster crown molding about 6 inches tall painted pale champagne, made of three flat stepped bands that step outward toward the top, crisp straight edges.
A smooth pale cream painted plaster ceiling of a 1920s office tower, clean and even, no pattern.

Back-of-house wall of a 1920s office tower radio station: smooth painted plaster in a dull institutional gray-green, scuffed and faintly grimy, a few small chips and pencil marks too faint to read, no pattern.
A 1920s plain brown battleship linoleum floor in large sheets, a flat chocolate brown with faint darker mottling, scuffed and worn dull in patches, one long thin seam crossing it.
A plain 1920s painted wooden baseboard about 5 inches tall in dark gray-green enamel, chipped along its top edge, a flat face with a squared top.

A wide radio studio window into a control room, about 7 feet wide and 4 feet tall: a thick double pane of plate glass set deep in a heavy dark walnut frame with a wide flat sill, two faint green edges where the glass panes meet the frame. The glass is completely transparent.

A heavy deep oxblood red velvet curtain drawn fully closed, about 9 feet wide and 6 and a half feet tall, hanging in deep vertical folds from brass rings on a round brass rod with ball finials at both ends, the hem just touching nothing below. Seen straight on, the curtain solid with no gaps.

A heavy 1920s radio studio door of solid dark oak, four tall flat panels and a small square window of clear glass at eye height, a brass knob on the right side, no lock and no keyhole, a plain dark oak casing. The window glass is completely transparent.

A split cast-iron door bar bracket, an open-topped U-shaped iron hook about 5 inches across that holds a wooden bar across a door, painted black, torn half out of the wood with its two long screws still in it and a pale splintered gouge in the oak frame behind. Seen straight on.

A square wooden access panel about 2 feet across set flush low in a wall, painted flat dark oxblood red, its edges a fine dark crack all around, no handle and no visible fastening on this side, a faint scuff along its bottom edge. Seen straight on.

A round 1920s Art Deco electric wall clock about 15 inches across, a black lacquered case with a stepped chrome bezel, a cream dial with bold black Arabic numerals 12, 3, 6 and 9 and plain black bars for the other hours, black hands and a thin red sweep second hand. Seen straight on.

Seen from directly above: a police chalk outline of a man lying face down on a dark bottle green carpet, arms bent up by the head, drawn in a rough broken white chalk line about an inch thick, with a large irregular dark brown stain near the head end that has been scrubbed at and lightened unevenly. Everything outside the chalk and the stain completely transparent.

The view through a thick studio window into a 1927 radio control room: a long control board of black panels with round dials, brass keys and two inset turntables right behind the glass, an empty high stool, gray-green walls, a pen recorder in a glass case on the far wall. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

A 1920s radio announcer's desk of dark satin walnut in a plain Art Deco shape, a flat top with rounded front corners, a solid modesty panel on the front and one shallow drawer, a green felt pad set into the top. 4 feet 6 inches wide, 2 feet 6 inches deep, 2 feet 6 inches tall. Upright.

A 1920s announcer's chair: a walnut armless side chair with a padded oxblood leather seat and a curved padded leather backrest held with brass tacks, tapered legs. 1 foot 7 inches wide, 1 foot 8 inches deep, 2 feet 10 inches tall. Upright, facing forward.
A 1920s desk lamp with a round brass base, a short brass stem and a dome-shaped green cased-glass shade, cream inside. 8 inches across the base, 14 inches tall. Upright, switched off.

A 1920s double-button carbon desk microphone: a round brass ring about 6 inches across holding a black button microphone on small coil springs in its center, on a short brass desk stand with a round black base. 7 inches across the base, 14 inches tall. Upright.

A short stack of typed radio script pages from 1927, about 8 and a half by 11 inches, lying flat and squared up, the top page typed in soft unreadable lines with a few pencil corrections and a yellow wooden pencil lying across it.

A tall 1920s radio amplifier rack: a black enameled steel cabinet open at the front holding four black panels with round black dials, small brass toggle switches and a few glass vacuum tubes in a row near the top, on four black iron casters. 2 feet 6 inches wide, 1 foot 9 inches deep, 6 feet 6 inches tall. Upright.

An 1890s double-hung window with a dark varnished oak casing, one pane in each sash, plain white muslin curtains tied back to each side and a dark green roller shade raised to the top, rain droplets on the glass. Every glass pane is completely transparent apart from the droplets.

The view from a ground-floor window on South Halsted Street in Chicago on a gray, rainy October day in 1927: the wide wet street with streetcar tracks and overhead wires, a streetcar going by, across the street a row of two- and three-story brick buildings with small shops under striped awnings and flats above, smoke from chimneys, a low gray sky. No readable signs. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

An 1890s front door of dark varnished oak with a tall oval of clear beveled glass in its upper half framed by a carved molding, one flat panel below, a brass knob and a brass key plate on the left side, a brass chain lock. The oval glass is completely transparent.

A small 1900s wooden key board on a wall, about 3 feet wide and 2 feet tall, dark varnished oak with two rows of brass hooks under small painted white numbers 1 to 10, a few iron room keys hanging on brass tags. Seen straight on.

An 1890s rooming house front desk: a tall dark varnished oak counter with a paneled front and a flat top, a small brass bell on the top, a few pigeonholes on the back side. 5 feet wide, 2 feet 6 inches deep, 3 feet 6 inches tall. Upright.

A large 1920s lodgers' register book, about 12 by 16 inches, bound in black cloth with red leather corners, lying open flat with columns of handwritten ink entries too small to read, a black wooden dip pen lying in the gutter.

An 1890s straight wooden staircase of dark varnished oak climbing to an upper floor, with a worn red carpet runner held by brass stair rods, a heavy turned newel post at the foot and turned balusters on the open side. 12 feet long, 3 feet 6 inches wide, 10 feet tall. Upright.

A 1920s square folding card table with a green baize top and dark wooden edges and legs, a worn deck of playing cards squared up in one corner and a small pencilled score pad with a pencil in another, the writing too small to read. 3 feet wide, 3 feet deep, 2 feet 6 inches tall. Upright.

A 1927 table radio receiver in a long low dark mahogany cabinet with three round dials and knobs in a row, on a small oak stand with a lower shelf, a separate black horn loudspeaker on top. 2 feet 6 inches wide, 1 foot 2 inches deep, 3 feet 6 inches tall. Upright, switched off.

An 1890s Victorian settee upholstered in worn dark red velvet with buttoned tufting on the back and a carved dark walnut frame, short carved legs, a white lace antimacassar on the back. 5 feet 6 inches wide, 2 feet 6 inches deep, 3 feet 2 inches tall. Upright.

A 1920s floor lamp with a brass column on a round weighted base and a wide pleated parchment shade with a fringe of small glass beads. 1 foot 8 inches across, 5 feet 4 inches tall. Upright, switched off.

An 1890s oak hall tree with a small beveled mirror, four brass coat hooks, a lift-lid bench seat and an umbrella holder with a drip tray, one black umbrella in it. 3 feet wide, 1 foot 4 inches deep, 6 feet 6 inches tall. Upright.

A 1920s riverside freight yard seen straight down: packed black cinders and gray gravel, wet, with shallow puddles, a few deep tire ruts, scattered straw and splinters, an old rusted bolt here and there.

The surroundings of a Chicago riverside freight yard looking toward the river on a gray October afternoon in 1927: the yard ends at a timber pier edge with heavy pilings, beyond it the green-gray Chicago River, a coal barge tied up, and across the water the steel trusses and lower deck of the Wells Street bridge with the elevated tracks on its upper deck, the dark Loop towers behind under a flat gray sky. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

The surroundings of a Chicago riverside freight yard looking toward the river late on a cold October night in 1927: the yard ends at a timber pier edge with heavy pilings, beyond it the black river with thin fog on the water, across the water the dark steel trusses of the Wells Street bridge with its round lamps, the elevated tracks on its upper deck, the lit windows of the Loop towers beyond under a black overcast sky. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

The surroundings of a Chicago freight yard looking back toward the street on a gray October afternoon in 1927: a tall iron-framed chain-link fence along Kinzie Street, across the cobbled street with its railroad spur track a row of soot-darkened brick warehouses and a coal dealer's shed, telegraph poles and wires, a flat gray sky. No readable signs. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

The surroundings of a Chicago freight yard looking back toward the street late on an October night in 1927: a tall iron-framed chain-link fence along Kinzie Street, across the wet cobbled street the black shapes of brick warehouses with no lit windows, one iron street lamp on the corner, telegraph poles and wires against a black overcast sky. No readable signs. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

The side of a Chicago riverside freight yard on a gray October afternoon in 1927: a tall gray weathered board fence topped with a strand of barbed wire, and over it the back of the next brick warehouse with a rusted iron fire escape and a tall brick chimney, a flat gray sky. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

The side of a Chicago riverside freight yard late on an October night in 1927: a tall dark board fence topped with a strand of barbed wire, and over it the black bulk of the next brick warehouse with a fire escape and a tall chimney against a black overcast sky. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

The long side of a two-story 1890s brick river warehouse seen straight on across a freight yard on a gray October afternoon in 1927: soot-dark red brick, a row of small iron-shuttered upper windows, a raised wooden loading dock along the bottom, and on the warehouse's street-end wall at the far right a big painted sign in faded white capitals, two lines that read exactly "RIVERSIDE SHIPPING" and "AND STORAGE CO." Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

The long side of a two-story 1890s brick river warehouse seen straight on across a freight yard late on an October night in 1927: black-red brick, a row of small dark upper windows, a raised wooden loading dock along the bottom, the painted sign on the far end wall too dark to read, a black overcast sky above the roofline. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

A wide 1890s warehouse river door about 10 feet wide and 10 feet tall: two leaves of heavy vertical planks weathered gray with black iron strap hinges, an iron hasp and staple at the middle, and the number "6" painted large in white in a plain stencil on the upper planks. Seen straight on, closed.

A wide 1890s warehouse river door about 10 feet wide and 10 feet tall: two leaves of heavy vertical planks weathered gray with black iron strap hinges, an iron hasp and staple at the middle, and the number "5" painted large in white in a plain stencil on the upper planks. Seen straight on, closed.

A wide 1890s warehouse river door about 10 feet wide and 10 feet tall: two leaves of heavy vertical planks weathered gray with black iron strap hinges, an iron hasp and staple at the middle, and the number "4" painted large in white in a plain stencil on the upper planks. Seen straight on, closed.

A 1920s freight yard gate: two swinging leaves of iron pipe frame filled with galvanized chain-link mesh, a strand of barbed wire along the top, hung on two square brick gate posts with stone caps, a heavy chain and padlock hanging open at the middle. 16 feet wide, 1 foot 6 inches deep, 8 feet tall. Upright, closed.

A 1920s watchman's shed: a small wooden shack of gray-painted clapboard with a tarpaper roof, a door with four small panes, a window with a shelf under it, a stovepipe through the roof, and an enameled iron gooseneck lamp on a bracket over the door. 7 feet wide, 6 feet deep, 9 feet tall. Upright.

A 1920s stake-bed freight truck: a black open cab with a flat roof, a long black hood with a radiator grille, solid black rubber tires on spoked steel wheels, and a long flat wooden bed with removable stake sides, mud-splashed. 6 feet 6 inches wide, 18 feet long, 8 feet tall. Upright.
A stack of eight 1920s wooden freight pallets of rough gray-weathered planks, slightly uneven, one corner splintered. 4 feet wide, 4 feet deep, 3 feet 6 inches tall. Upright.
A group of three 1920s wooden barrels with black iron hoops standing on end, weathered gray-brown, one with its lid nailed down. 4 feet wide, 3 feet deep, 3 feet tall. Upright.

A 12-foot section of a 1890s timber river pier edge: a heavy timber curb along the top of thick tarred wooden pilings, three pilings showing, and a squat black cast-iron mooring bollard bolted to the timber. 12 feet wide, 2 feet deep, 3 feet tall.

A heavy iron chain about 3 feet long hung through a warehouse door hasp, with a large black iron padlock locked through two of its links, the chain slightly rusted. 1 foot wide, 6 inches deep, 3 feet tall. Hanging straight down.

A 1926 black four-door Packard sedan: a long black hood with a tall nickel radiator shell, two large nickel headlamps, sweeping black fenders and running boards, wooden-spoked wheels with white sidewall tires, a black square-backed closed body with a small oval rear window. 6 feet wide, 16 feet long, 6 feet tall. Upright.

The inside wall of an 1890s river warehouse: old common red brick in running bond, coated with flaking grayish whitewash that has worn away in patches to show the dull red brick, bricks about 8 inches long, a few rust stains, no pattern beyond the brick.
An 1890s warehouse floor of wide heavy pine planks about 8 inches across, worn gray and gouged by hand trucks and crates, dark oil stains, scattered bits of straw and wood splinters.

An 1890s warehouse ceiling looking straight up: heavy rough-sawn timber joists about 10 inches deep set about 2 feet apart, running in one direction, with the gray underside of the plank floor above showing between them, dusty and cobwebbed.
A 1920s warehouse light seen from directly below: a bare clear bulb inside a round wire cage guard, hanging from a black porcelain socket on a cloth-covered cord, switched off.

A small 1890s warehouse window about 3 feet wide and 3 and a half feet tall: a grimy wooden frame with four small panes, one cracked, and close behind the glass on the outside, rough gray planks nailed across it with uneven gaps about an inch wide between them. The glass is completely transparent and the gaps between the planks are completely transparent.

The view through narrow gaps between boards over a second-floor warehouse window on the Chicago River late on a cold October night in 1927: far below, the black water of the river moving fast with thin fog on it, and across it the dark steel trusses of the Wells Street bridge with its round lamps lit in a row and the elevated tracks on its upper deck, the black overcast sky. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

An 1890s warehouse door of rough vertical pine planks held by two black iron Z braces and black strap hinges, a plain iron thumb latch on the right side, grimy and worn at the latch. Seen straight on, closed.

An 1890s warehouse inner door of rough vertical soft pine planks held by black iron Z braces and black strap hinges, a plain iron thumb latch on the left side, no lock of its own. Seen straight on, closed.
A cheap 1920s steel hasp and staple screwed into soft pine, with a small brass padlock locked through the staple, the screws bright and short, seen straight on.

A 1920s wooden packing crate of rough pale pine boards, nailed shut, bound around with two thin flat steel bands, one band snapped with its broken end curled up and sharp. 3 feet wide, 2 feet 6 inches deep, 2 feet 6 inches tall. Upright.
A stack of three 1920s wooden packing crates of rough pale pine, nailed shut, the biggest on the bottom, plain with no stencils, dusty. 3 feet wide, 2 feet 6 inches deep, 5 feet tall. Upright.

A small open cardboard box of 1920s manila shipping tags with white string threaded through their reinforced holes, the tags blank, and a short flat carpenter's pencil stub about 2 inches long lying beside it. 8 inches wide, 5 inches deep, 4 inches tall.

A plain 1910s wooden kitchen chair of unpainted pine with three back spindles, scuffed, a short loose length of cut hemp rope lying on its seat. 1 foot 5 inches wide, 1 foot 6 inches deep, 3 feet tall. Upright, facing forward.

An 1890s warehouse office window about 3 and a half feet wide and 4 and a half feet tall: a grimy wooden double-hung frame with six panes in each sash, a narrow sill, a little soot in the corners. Every glass pane is completely transparent.

The view from a second-floor warehouse office window right over the Chicago River late on a cold October night in 1927: the black river directly below, moving fast with thin fog, and across it the Wells Street bridge, its steel trusses and its row of round lamps lit, the elevated tracks on the upper deck, a walkway along the rail on the lower deck, the lit Loop towers beyond. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

A 1920s night watchman's electric hand lamp hanging from an iron hook on a wall: a black-painted steel box body with a wire bail handle on top, a round glass lens on its front with a sliding black metal shutter half across it, switched off. Seen straight on.

An open 1890s warehouse doorway in a whitewashed brick wall with a plain rough timber frame, no door, and beyond it the top of a steep narrow wooden stair going straight down into the dark, a worn handrail of plain pipe on one side. Everything inside the frame is completely transparent.

The view through an open doorway down a steep narrow wooden warehouse stair at night in 1927: worn plank treads going straight down between whitewashed brick walls to a plank floor below, the dark shapes of stacked crates at the bottom. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

A plain 1910s tally clerk's desk of scuffed pine with a slanted writing top over a shallow drawer, a flat shelf along its back, four square legs, stained with ink. 4 feet wide, 2 feet 6 inches deep, 3 feet 2 inches tall. Upright.

A thick 1920s ledger bound in green cloth with brown leather corners and spine and no title on the cover, lying open flat at handwritten columns of dates and dollar figures in ink too small to read. About 11 by 15 inches and 2 inches thick.

A small 1920s gooseneck desk lamp of black-painted steel with a round weighted base, a flexible neck and a cone-shaped black metal shade. 6 inches across the base, 14 inches tall. Upright, switched off.
A tall plain 1910s clerk's stool of unpainted pine with a square seat and four splayed legs joined by rungs, scuffed. 1 foot 2 inches across, 2 feet 8 inches tall. Upright.

A 1920s wooden shipping crate of rough pale pine boards, nailed shut, stenciled on its front side in black block capitals on three lines that read exactly "RADIO CABINETS." then "BAY 6." then "RIVER DOOR." 3 feet wide, 2 feet deep, 2 feet 6 inches tall. Upright.

A set of plain 1910s pine shelves holding rows of thin tally books, bundles of blank tally sheets tied with string and a tin box of pencils, no readable labels. 4 feet wide, 1 foot 2 inches deep, 6 feet tall. Upright.

A wide 1890s warehouse river door seen from inside, about 10 feet wide and 10 feet tall: two leaves of heavy vertical gray-weathered planks with black iron strap hinges and diagonal braces, two heavy black iron U-shaped brackets bolted across the middle to take a timber bar, empty, and a thin line of darkness along the bottom edge. Seen straight on, closed.

The view out through an open warehouse river door late on a cold October night in 1927: a narrow timber pier with heavy pilings right outside, the black Chicago River beyond with fog on it, to the left along the pilings the iron stairs climbing to the Wells Street bridge with its lit round lamps, and to the right, up the yard, a single lamp over a small watchman's shed by a chain-link gate. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

An open 1890s warehouse doorway in a whitewashed brick wall with a rough timber frame, no door, and beyond it the bottom of a steep narrow wooden stair climbing straight up into the dark, a plain pipe handrail on one side. Everything inside the frame is completely transparent.

The view through an open doorway up a steep narrow wooden warehouse stair at night in 1927: worn plank treads climbing straight up between whitewashed brick walls to a dark landing and a doorway at the top. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.
A heavy squared timber door bar of rough dark pine about 11 feet long, 9 inches tall and 6 inches thick, its ends worn smooth and darkened by hands. Lying flat on its wide side.

A stack of six 1920s wooden shipping crates of rough pale pine in two rows of three, each stenciled in black block capitals exactly "RADIO CABINETS", nailed shut, a few wisps of straw sticking out of the joints. 6 feet wide, 3 feet deep, 6 feet tall. Upright.

A 1920s two-wheeled warehouse hand truck with a wooden frame, long curved handles, a steel nose plate and two iron-rimmed wheels, standing upright. 2 feet wide, 1 foot 6 inches deep, 4 feet 6 inches tall. Upright.
A big coil of heavy brown manila mooring rope about 2 inches thick, coiled flat on the floor in neat rings, a little frayed at the end. 3 feet across, 1 foot tall.

A 1920s bridge sidewalk deck seen straight down: wet heavy timber planks about 10 inches wide laid crosswise with narrow dark gaps, worn smooth and dark gray, black iron bolt heads in rows along them.

Looking across the Chicago River from the Wells Street bridge rail late on a cold October night in 1927: the black water below with thin fog, and on the far bank the long dark back of a two-story brick warehouse running along the water, a row of twelve plank river doors shut along a timber pier, and upstairs at the near end two windows side by side, one boarded over and one a dark square of glass. A few distant lamps, a black overcast sky. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

Looking back across the lower deck of the Wells Street bridge in Chicago late on an October night in 1927: the wet roadway with streetcar tracks, heavy riveted steel trusses and girders, the underside of the elevated railway deck overhead with its cross beams, round bridge lamps lit along the truss, the far sidewalk railing. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

Looking south along the sidewalk of the Wells Street bridge in Chicago late on an October night in 1927: the riveted steel truss and railing running ahead to the Loop end of the bridge, the bridge tender's small house with a dark window, the tall office towers of the Loop beyond with a few lit windows, a black overcast sky. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

Looking north along the sidewalk of the Wells Street bridge in Chicago late on an October night in 1927: the riveted steel truss and railing running ahead to the north bank, low brick warehouses along the river, the head of iron stairs going down to the riverbank by the rail, a cab rank with two black taxicabs under a street lamp at the end. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

A 10-foot section of a 1920s steel bridge railing: a black-painted riveted steel top rail and bottom rail with a lattice of flat crossed steel bars between them, on short square posts at each end. 10 feet wide, 8 inches deep, 3 feet 8 inches tall. Upright.
A 1920s Chicago bridge lamp post: a fluted black cast-iron column on a square base with a single round white glass globe on top, switched off. 1 foot 6 inches across the base, 11 feet tall. Upright.

The top of a 1920s iron stair down from a bridge to a riverbank: a black-painted steel stair opening in the deck with a steep flight of open steel treads going down, flanked by black pipe handrails curving over at the top. 4 feet wide, 6 feet long, 3 feet 6 inches tall. Upright.
