A modern white plastic rocker light switch on a plain white rectangular wall plate with no visible screws, the rocker pressed down at the bottom. The plate is about 3 by 4.75 inches.

A suspended acoustic tile ceiling of 2 by 2 foot white mineral fiber tiles with a fine fissured texture, held in a thin white metal grid; the grid lines run in both directions every 2 feet, so a 4 foot tile shows exactly two tiles each way. Clean and nearly new.
A 2 by 2 foot recessed LED flat panel light seen from directly below, switched off: a thin white aluminum frame around a smooth, even, pale gray-white acrylic diffuser.
A 4 inch commercial vinyl cove base in dark charcoal gray, matte, with a small curved toe at the bottom where it meets the floor and a straight top edge.
Commercial carpet tile in a muted blue-gray loop pile with a faint darker linear striation, laid in 2 foot squares turned a quarter turn each so the seams are just visible; lightly worn, clean.
A 1920s schoolhouse pendant light seen from directly below, switched off: a round white opal glass globe about 14 inches across, its opening ringed by a small brushed brass fitter.

A closed manila private investigator's case folder lying flat, 9 by 12 inches, about an inch thick, a printed white label on its tab that reads exactly "SAYER, B.", the corner of a printed email and a single register page sticking out of one side.
A closed laboratory report folder in pale gray card, 9 by 12 inches, lying flat, a typed white label on the front with soft, unreadable text and a strip of red evidence seal tape across the flap.
A plain white letter-size envelope lying flat, hand-addressed in blue ink with soft, unreadable writing, a stamp and a round postmark in the corner, slightly creased.
A buff 10 by 13 inch government envelope lying flat, a typed white routing label with soft, unreadable text and a strip of red evidence tape across the flap.
A white cardboard banker's file box with its lid on, 15 inches long, 12 inches wide and 10 inches high, hand holes at each end, a typed summary sheet clipped to the lid with soft, unreadable text.
A closed blue three-ring binder, 10 by 11 and a half inches, lying flat, with a white printed label on the cover that reads exactly "FINAL REPORT".
The inside wall of a 1940s brick colonial house in Arlington, Virginia: smooth painted plaster in a soft warm white with a hint of cream, eggshell finish, very slightly aged and evenly kept.
A 1940s red oak strip floor, 2 and a quarter inch boards running in one direction, a mid-brown satin finish lightly worn along a walking path, staggered board ends, tight seams.
A smooth painted plaster ceiling in flat white, slightly aged, no texture.
A painted colonial baseboard about 5 and a half inches high, semi-gloss white, a flat board with a small ogee cap along the top and a quarter-round shoe at the bottom.
A simple painted colonial crown molding about 4 inches high, semi-gloss white, a classic cove and bead profile.
A 1990s flush-mount ceiling light seen from directly below, switched off: a round frosted white glass dome about 13 inches across held by a small brushed nickel finial in the center.

A 1940s wooden double-hung window painted white, six panes over six panes, a brass sash lock, a plain white roller shade pulled up to the top of the frame, white painted casing and a narrow sill. Every glass pane is completely transparent.

The view from the front window of a brick colonial on North 19th Street in Arlington, Virginia, on a gray, damp late-December morning in 2018: a small front yard with boxwoods and a brick walk, then a quiet residential street of two-story red brick colonials with white trim and covered porches, tall bare oaks along both curbs, strings of unlit Christmas lights still on half the porch rails, a wreath on a door, a few parked 2010s sedans, and an empty stretch of curb directly across the street. Flat gray winter sky. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

A 1940s wooden double-hung kitchen window painted white, a single pane in each sash, a short white cafe curtain on a thin brass rod across the lower half, white casing. Every glass pane is completely transparent.

The view from a kitchen window at the back of a brick colonial in Arlington, Virginia, on a gray late-December morning in 2018: a small backyard of dormant brown grass with leaves along the edges, a bird feeder on a pole, a bare dogwood, a weathered wooden privacy fence with a gate open onto a narrow paved back alley, and over the fence the back of the neighboring brick house with its own kitchen window and a closed curtain. Flat gray sky. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

An open interior doorway in a white painted colonial casing, the six-panel white door swung fully open and out of sight, so the doorway itself is an empty opening. The opening inside the casing is completely transparent.

The view through an open doorway into a tidy small bedroom of a 1940s Arlington colonial on a late-December morning in 2018: a made double bed with a navy quilt and two pillows squared off, a wooden dresser with its top two drawers pulled half open and a few socks visible inside, a folding wooden luggage stand standing empty against the wall, and a closet with its door open showing hanging shirts with a clear gap about two feet wide in the middle. Cream walls, oak floor, a small rag rug. Packed quickly but neatly. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.
A closed 1940s six-panel interior door painted semi-gloss white with a round brass knob on the left side, in a white colonial casing. Seen from inside the room.
A small framed watercolor print of a male northern cardinal perched on a snowy holly branch, in a narrow walnut frame with a cream mat, about 14 by 18 inches, no readable text.

A tall freestanding wooden bookcase in dark cherry stain, 3 feet wide, 12 inches deep and 7 feet high, five shelves filled with cookbooks, field guides to birds, a run of matching county history volumes, and on the middle shelf a plain gray three-ring binder with a small label-maker strip on its spine, soft and unreadable. Neat, every book upright.
A plain 1980s oak writing desk, 4 feet wide, 2 feet deep and 30 inches high, a single shallow center drawer and an open knee space beneath, its top cleared to the bare wood.
A simple brushed brass swing-arm desk lamp with a small cone shade, about 16 inches high, switched off.
A yellow legal pad lying flat, 8 and a half by 11 and three quarters inches, the top sheet torn away leaving a ragged fringe at the binding, the next sheet blank.

A small fireproof document safe in charcoal gray steel, 16 inches wide, 13 inches deep and 12 inches high, its door standing wide open, empty inside except a gray foam lining that still holds a shallow rectangular hollow about the size of a paperback book.

A small flush-mount ceiling light seen from directly below, switched off: a round polished brass ring about 18 inches across holding a frosted white glass bowl, a small brass finial at the center, a ring of small clear crystal drops around the edge.

A tall classical prewar window, about 4 and a half feet wide and 8 feet high: a white-painted wooden casement pair with three panes per side, a deep paneled reveal, cream silk curtains tied back at each side. Every glass pane is completely transparent.

The view from a high floor of a prewar building at 1140 Fifth Avenue, New York, on a cold late-December day in 2018 after snow: Fifth Avenue below with yellow cabs and black cars in the slush, a dark green canvas awning directly below with a doorman in a long coat brushing snow off it, and across the avenue the low stone wall of Central Park and the park beyond, bare trees and white lawns, the reservoir and the far towers of the West Side under a flat pale gray sky. Seen from about 100 feet up.

A small framed photograph in a thin gilt frame with a cream mat, about 11 by 14 inches: six people in good coats standing on the stone steps of a Washington townhouse, squinting toward the viewer, a woman in her early forties with short dark hair in the center; on the mat below the photograph a small engraved brass label that reads exactly "Meridian Advisory Group, 2007".

A group of four framed award plaques and certificates hung in a neat two-by-two grid, walnut and brass, with small brass plates and printed text all soft and unreadable, the whole group about 4 feet wide and 3 feet high.

A framed photograph of a grant ceremony in a thin black frame with a white mat, about 20 by 16 inches: a row of smiling people in suits holding an oversized check on a stage, the check's writing soft and unreadable.

A closed tall paneled office door painted soft cream, six raised panels, a polished brass lever handle on the right side, in a classical molded cream casing with a small cornice above. Seen from outside the office.

A pair of closed tall paneled double doors painted soft cream, each with four raised panels and a polished brass lever handle meeting in the middle, in a classical molded cream casing. Seen from inside the room.

A long formal boardroom table in polished dark mahogany, 16 feet long, 4 and a half feet wide and 30 inches high, on two carved pedestal bases, its top laid with neat rows of black three-ring binders, each tabbed along the edge with colored tabs, and two short stacks of white file boxes at one end.
A formal boardroom armchair in dark mahogany with a seat and back upholstered in oxblood leather with brass nailhead trim, about 24 inches wide, 24 inches deep and 38 inches high.

An elegant traditional writing desk in mahogany with tapered legs and a tooled dark green leather top, 5 feet wide, 2 and a half feet deep and 30 inches high, holding a slim monitor, a cordless phone in its base, a leather blotter, and a small leather out tray with a white courier envelope lying face down in it.
A traditional upholstered desk chair in mahogany with a seat and back in cream damask, on four legs with small brass casters, about 22 inches wide and 36 inches high.
A narrow classical console table in mahogany with a marble top, 5 feet long, 16 inches deep and 32 inches high, holding a tall vase of white amaryllis.
A formal camelback sofa upholstered in pale gray-green silk with dark mahogany legs, 7 feet long, 3 feet deep and 34 inches high.
The wall of a sleek 2010s Manhattan corner law office: smooth painted drywall in a light dove gray, flat matte, immaculate.
A dense wool-blend office carpet in deep charcoal with a very faint tone-on-tone small square texture, clean and new.
A smooth painted drywall ceiling in flat white, perfectly plain.
A slim 4 inch modern baseboard in dark walnut with a satin finish and a crisp square top edge.
A 4-foot linear recessed ceiling light seen from directly below, switched off: a narrow white aluminum channel about 5 inches wide with a smooth white frosted diffuser.

A floor-to-ceiling office curtain-wall window, about 6 feet wide and 9 and a half feet high, one tall pane above a low narrow spandrel strip, in slim dark gray aluminum mullions. The glass is completely transparent.

The view from the fortieth floor of a Lexington Avenue tower in Midtown Manhattan on a short late-December afternoon in 2018: the Chrysler Building close by with its stepped steel crown, the glass and stone towers of Midtown around it, water towers on older rooftops below, and a pale gray winter sky. Seen from about 450 feet up.

The view east from the fortieth floor of a Lexington Avenue tower in Midtown Manhattan on a short late-December afternoon in 2018: the slab of the United Nations headquarters, the gray East River, Roosevelt Island and the low buildings of Queens beyond, Midtown rooftops below, a pale gray winter sky. Seen from about 450 feet up.
A closed tall modern office door of dark walnut veneer, flush, with a long brushed stainless pull handle on the left side, in a slim dark gray metal frame. Seen from inside the office.

A neat group of three framed diplomas and law certificates in matching thin black frames with white mats, hung in a row, their printed text and seals soft and unreadable, the group about 5 feet wide and 1 and a half feet high.

A tall built-in style bookcase in dark walnut, 4 feet wide, 14 inches deep and 8 feet high, five shelves of corporate law treatises in matching maroon and navy bindings, trust and estates volumes and a row of bound minute books with names on their spines, soft and unreadable, with two clear gaps where binders were taken out.

A wide modern executive desk with a thick clear glass top on a dark walnut and brushed steel base, 6 and a half feet wide, 3 feet deep and 30 inches high, holding a slim monitor, a leather-bound notebook, a single pen and a closed laptop, otherwise clear.
A modern high-back executive chair in black leather on a polished aluminum five-star base with casters, about 26 inches wide and 44 inches high.
A modern guest armchair in black leather on a slim polished chrome cantilever frame, about 23 inches wide, 24 inches deep and 32 inches high.

A low dark walnut credenza with flush sliding doors and a lock on the center door, 6 feet long, 20 inches deep and 26 inches high, holding a small framed bar admission certificate leaning upright and a dead white orchid in a white ceramic pot, its stems bare and its leaves drooping.
The wall of a 2010s office suite in a Tysons, Virginia office tower: smooth painted drywall in a cool light gray, eggshell finish, spotless.

A wide modern office window, about 8 feet wide and 5 and a half feet high, two large panes in dark gray aluminum mullions, white horizontal mini-blinds drawn up into a slim headrail. The glass is completely transparent.

The view from a sixth-floor office window in Tysons, Virginia, on a gray late-December day in 2018: the wide lanes of the Leesburg Pike below with traffic, the raised concrete guideway of the Metro Silver Line running along it on tall piers, a multistory concrete mall parking deck, glass office towers, and directly below a surface parking lot with one empty reserved space whose painted curb stop reads exactly "PRS". Overcast sky. Seen from about 65 feet up.

A wall-mounted office whiteboard in a silver aluminum frame, about 6 feet wide and 4 feet high, half wiped: smeared gray streaks across the left half, and on the right half handwritten names, a street address, a short column of notes, a circled item and an arrow pointing up, all in black and red marker and all soft and unreadable, a marker tray with an eraser at the bottom.

A closed office suite door of medium cherry veneer, flush, with a brushed steel lever handle on the right side and a small electronic card reader beside it, in a dark gray metal frame. Seen from inside the office.

A neat group of four framed military service plaques and certificates in dark wood and brass hung in a straight row: a Military Police Corps crossed-pistols emblem, a retirement certificate, a unit plaque and a framed photograph of a squad of soldiers, all small text soft and unreadable, the group about 5 feet wide and 1 and a half feet high.

A triangular wooden flag display case in dark cherry with a clear glass front, about 2 feet wide and 1 foot high, holding a tightly folded United States flag showing the blue field and white stars. The glass is completely transparent.

A severe 2010s executive desk with a dark gray steel frame and a black laminate top, 6 feet wide, 3 feet deep and 30 inches high, a locking pedestal of drawers on one side, its top bare except a black leather desk blotter, a desk phone and a closed laptop squared exactly to the edge.
A red file folder lying flat, 9 by 12 inches and about half an inch thick, with a typed white label on its tab that reads exactly "PITTSBURGH".
A black leather executive swivel chair with a high back and a black five-star base on casters, about 26 inches wide and 44 inches high.
A plain black leather guest chair on a black steel sled base, about 22 inches wide, 23 inches deep and 33 inches high.
An indoor United States flag on a polished wooden pole with a brass eagle finial, the flag hanging in neat folds, the pole in a weighted brass floor stand, about 8 feet tall.
A four-drawer lateral steel file cabinet in black, 3 feet wide, 20 inches deep and 52 inches high, each drawer with a small lock.

Six white cardboard file boxes with lids stacked in two columns of three, each about 15 by 12 by 10 inches, each lid crossed with a strip of red evidence tape and marked with a handwritten number on a white label, soft and unreadable.
The wall of an old windowless trust company records room in a 1920s Wilmington, Delaware office building: smooth painted plaster in a muted sage gray, matte, old and very evenly kept.
Old battleship gray linoleum with a faint darker mottling, laid in large sheets, waxed to a soft dull sheen, a little worn along the aisles.
An old painted plaster ceiling in ivory, smooth, slightly aged.
A 1920s baseboard about 7 inches high in dark stained oak with a simple rounded cap, the varnish old and mellow.
A plain 1920s plaster cove crown molding about 5 inches high, painted ivory, with one narrow flat band along its lower edge.

A closed heavy 1920s office door of dark stained oak with a single tall recessed panel, a brass lever handle and a brass deadbolt on the right side, in a plain oak casing, and a small brass plate above the handle that reads exactly "RECORDS". Seen from inside the room.

A brown hardboard clipboard hanging on a brass hook, its clip holding a ruled sign-out sheet with columns of handwritten entries, soft and unreadable, a ballpoint pen on a chain. About 9 by 12 and a half inches.
A plain round institutional wall clock about 14 inches across with a black rim, a white face, black numerals 1 to 12 and black hands at ten past ten.

A bank of mobile high-density filing shelves in beige-painted steel on floor rails, 12 feet long, 8 feet deep (three carriages pushed together) and 7 and a half feet high, a round three-spoke turning handle on the end panel of each carriage, the shelves packed with red-rope expanding files each tied with a cord and tagged with a small white label.
A plain oak library reading table, 5 feet long, 3 feet wide and 30 inches high, on four square tapered legs, worn smooth on the top.

A red-rope expanding file folder lying flat, 10 by 15 inches and about 3 inches thick, its flap open and its string tie loose, a white tag on the cord with soft unreadable writing, three bright yellow tabs sticking out of the papers inside.

A long oak library reading table, 10 feet long, 3 and a half feet wide and 30 inches high, holding two classic green glass-shaded brass banker's lamps switched off, a desk calculator printing a long curl of white paper tape, a yellow legal pad covered in penciled columns of figures, and a pencil.
A sturdy 1920s oak library chair with a curved back rail, vertical spindles and a solid seat, about 19 inches wide and 33 inches high.
An old oak card catalog cabinet of fifteen small drawers with brass label holders and pulls, 3 feet wide, 18 inches deep and 4 feet high, on a plain base.
The wall of a 2010s forensic document laboratory: smooth painted drywall in a clean bright white with a faint cool gray tint, eggshell finish, spotless.
Light gray seamless sheet vinyl laboratory flooring with a fine white and darker gray speckle, smooth with a soft sheen, clean.

A modern office window, about 6 and a half feet wide and 4 and a half feet high, in a white aluminum frame, completely covered by closed white horizontal mini-blinds with their slats turned shut and a thin wand at one side.

A closed laboratory door of light gray laminate, flush, with a narrow vertical wire-glass vision panel, a brushed steel lever handle on the right side and a small electronic keypad lock above it, in a white steel frame. The vision panel glass is completely transparent.
The view through a narrow door vision panel into a plain white laboratory corridor with gray sheet vinyl floor and a closed door opposite. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.
A row of wall-hung white laminate laboratory upper cabinets, about 8 feet wide and 3 feet high, four doors with slim brushed steel bar pulls.
A framed handwriting comparison reference chart in a thin black frame, about 2 by 3 feet, rows of enlarged handwritten letter forms and signature samples, soft and unreadable.

A long laboratory workbench, 10 feet wide, 3 feet deep and 36 inches high, with a gray epoxy resin top and a white steel cabinet base, holding two desktop workstation towers with two flat monitors each showing soft gray unreadable windows, a small black forensic write-blocker box with cables, a sealed clear plastic evidence bag holding a ruggedized external drive, a paper log book, and an adjustable articulated task lamp switched off.

A forensic comparison microscope on its own small gray epoxy-topped lab table: two matched microscope bodies joined by an optical bridge to a single binocular eyepiece, black and white enamel with chrome focusing knobs, the whole about 3 feet wide, 2 feet deep and 4 feet high including the table.
A long document light table, 14 feet long, 4 feet deep and 36 inches high, a flat frosted white glass top in a brushed aluminum frame on white steel legs, the top bare, switched off.
A laboratory stool with a black padded seat, a short backrest, a chrome foot ring and a five-star base on casters, about 20 inches across and 36 inches high.
A plain modern stacking chair with a charcoal plastic shell seat on a chrome four-leg frame, about 20 inches wide and 32 inches high.

A thick printed register, about 2 and a half inches thick, of letter-size pages held by black binder clips at the top, lying flat, a dense row of small red tabs along its right edge, the top page showing columns of soft unreadable entries and codes.

A neat stack of photocopies of short typed notes on plain white letter-size paper, about an inch thick, lying flat, the top page showing a few soft unreadable typed lines and a single inked handwritten letter at the bottom.

A small spread of three or four letter-size printed pages laid flat and slightly fanned, stapled at the corner, typed forms and tables with boxes, soft and unreadable, a few ink marks and initials in the boxes.
Six small white specimen signature cards, each about 3 by 5 inches, laid flat in a straight row, each with a typed line and an inked signature, soft and unreadable; the row about 20 inches long.
The upper wall of an old Manhattan police station house squad room: painted plaster in a pale institutional cream-green, flat finish, a little dingy, with faint scuffs and a few patched spots.
The lower wall of an old Manhattan police station house: painted plaster in a darker institutional green, glossy enamel finish, scuffed and chipped in small spots from chair backs.
Worn 12 inch vinyl composition floor tiles in speckled beige and tan, laid in a grid with a few darker replacement tiles, scuffed by chair casters, waxed to a dull sheen.
A suspended acoustic ceiling of old 2 by 4 foot mineral fiber tiles, faintly yellowed, a couple with water stains, in a dull white metal grid, the long tiles running one way.
A 4 inch black rubber cove base, scuffed and slightly wavy, with a small curved toe at the bottom.
A plain flat wooden chair rail about 3 inches high, painted the same glossy dark green as the wall below it, chipped along the top edge.

A large office whiteboard used as a case board, about 6 feet wide and 4 feet high, in a silver aluminum frame: a photograph of a gray-haired man in a suit taped at upper left, a printed map of a few Midtown Manhattan blocks, a booking photograph of a heavyset man, lines of black marker notes, soft and unreadable, and across the upper right corner in large red marker the word "CHARGED", with underneath it in smaller black marker "Who sent him?"

An old steel-framed police station window, about 4 feet wide and 6 feet high, painted dark green, two sashes of wire glass with a fine diamond wire mesh embedded in clear glass. The glass between the wires is completely transparent.

The view through a police station window in Manhattan on a gray December day in 2018: a black iron fire escape landing with its ladder right outside the glass, and six feet beyond it a sooty red brick wall of the next building with a few small barred windows and a rusted drainpipe, a narrow slice of gray sky at the top. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.
An old cast-iron steam radiator, about 4 feet long and 2 and a half feet high, many vertical column sections, painted cream over older layers of paint, a valve handle at one end.
A cork bulletin board about 4 feet wide and 3 feet high in a plain wood frame, crowded with pinned memos, wanted flyers and schedules, all soft and unreadable.

A closed old wooden squad room door, painted dark green, with a large upper panel of clear wire glass and a brass knob on the left side, in a dark green painted casing. The glass is completely transparent.

The view through a wire-glass door panel into the hallway of an old Manhattan police station house: cream-green walls, a wooden bench, a bulletin board, a stairwell rail, worn beige tile floor. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

A cluttered old gray steel police detective's desk, 5 feet wide, 2 and a half feet deep and 30 inches high: a flat monitor and keyboard, a black desk phone, stacks of manila case folders, a coffee mug full of pens, a paper coffee cup, a nameplate holder with soft unreadable letters.
An old gray steel office desk, 5 feet wide, 2 and a half feet deep and 30 inches high, with a flat monitor, a keyboard, a phone and a few folders, slightly less cluttered.
A worn black vinyl office swivel chair with padded arms and a five-star base on casters, about 25 inches wide and 38 inches high.
A plain gray steel office side chair with a padded black vinyl seat and back, about 19 inches wide and 32 inches high.
A tall four-drawer vertical steel filing cabinet in tan, 15 inches wide, 28 inches deep and 52 inches high, dented, with a few stacked file boxes on top.
A small gray steel utility table, 3 feet wide, 18 inches deep and 30 inches high, holding a glass-carafe drip coffee maker, a stack of foam cups and a sugar canister.
A freestanding bentwood coat rack, about 6 feet high, with two dark coats and a scarf hanging on its hooks.
The wall of a modern federal office floor: smooth painted drywall in a cool pale gray, eggshell finish, clean and institutional.
Navy blue commercial carpet tile with a fine gray fleck and a faint linear texture, laid in 2 foot squares, clean and slightly worn along the walkways.

A wide modern office window, about 10 feet wide and 5 and a half feet high, three tall panes in dark gray aluminum mullions, white horizontal mini-blinds drawn up into a slim headrail, a deep sill. The glass is completely transparent.

The view from an upper-floor window of 601 4th Street NW, Washington, D.C., on a gray December day in 2018: Judiciary Square with bare trees and patchy grass, the long red brick bulk of the National Building Museum with its arched windows, the stone courthouses around the square, and at the curb below a line of black SUVs. Overcast sky. Seen from about 60 feet up.

A very large wall-mounted flat-panel video conference screen, about 7 feet wide and 4 feet high, in a thin black bezel, switched off, the screen an even dark gray, with a small black camera bar mounted on top.

A modern office door with a full-height clear glass panel in a slim dark gray aluminum frame, standing fully open into the small room beyond and out of sight, so only the frame and the empty doorway show. The opening is completely transparent.

The view through an open doorway into a small FBI video interview room, 2018: gray acoustic panels on the walls, a small gray table with two chairs facing a large flat screen on the far wall, a video camera on a tripod and a desk microphone on the table, a box of tissues. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.

A closed modern office door of light gray laminate, flush, with a narrow vertical clear glass vision panel, a brushed steel lever handle on the right side and a small card reader beside it, in a dark gray steel frame. The vision panel glass is completely transparent.
The view through a narrow door vision panel into a plain federal office corridor: pale gray walls, navy carpet, a closed door opposite. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.
A framed round emblem in a plain dark wood frame, about 2 feet across, a simplified blue and gold circle with a shield and laurel branches, with no readable words.

A long modern conference table with a dark gray laminate top and a brushed steel base, 14 feet long, 4 and a half feet wide and 30 inches high, a few closed folders, a laptop and a conference speakerphone on it.
A 2010s black mesh conference chair with a black seat, plastic armrests and a five-star base on casters, about 25 inches wide and 40 inches high.

A 2010s office workstation desk in gray laminate with low gray fabric privacy panels on two sides, 6 feet wide, 2 and a half feet deep and 30 inches high, a flat monitor, a keyboard, a desk phone and a short stack of binders.
A two-drawer lateral steel security file cabinet in dark gray, 3 feet wide, 20 inches deep and 28 inches high, each drawer with a combination lock dial, a small potted plant on top.

The inside wall of a 1920s converted printing plant in Long Island City: old common red brick in running bond, whitewashed long ago, the whitewash worn thin and chipped so the red brick and mortar show through in patches, with faint old ink smudges.
An old concrete factory floor, gray and pitted, with old printer's ink stains soaked in as black and blue-black blotches, swept.
A 1920s reinforced concrete slab ceiling painted white long ago, the paint flaking in small patches to gray concrete, a faint grid of formwork board marks.

An old industrial pendant light seen from directly below, switched off: a round white porcelain-enamel steel dome shade about 16 inches across with a chipped dark rim and a bare bulb socket in the center.

A tall steel-framed factory window, about 6 feet wide and 9 and a half feet high, a grid of small panes in a black painted steel frame, the lower half of the panes painted over flat gray-white, the upper half clear, a small pivot sash in the middle. The clear panes are completely transparent.

The view from a fourth-floor factory window on Skillman Avenue, Long Island City, Queens, on a gray December morning in 2018: the wide tracks and parked trains of the Sunnyside rail yards below, overhead catenary wires, old brick warehouses and new glass apartment towers around the yards, and across the East River the long Manhattan skyline with the Empire State Building and the Chrysler Building under a flat gray sky. Seen from about 50 feet up.
A closed old wide factory door of heavy wooden boards with a steel kick plate, painted dull gray-green and chipped, a steel lever latch on the left side, in a steel frame. Seen from inside the room.

A white work ticket taped up by two strips of clear tape, about 8 by 5 inches, with printed lines and black ink handwriting that reads exactly, on four lines: "On-site shredding.", "Mon 12/31, 7:00 AM.", "31 + 1 cartons.", "Bill to Pike Risk Services."

A closed old freight elevator gate, about 8 feet wide and 8 feet high: a vertically sliding steel door pair painted dark gray, the upper door with a small wire-glass window, a heavy canvas pull strap, in a steel frame. The wire-glass window is completely transparent.
A 1920s reinforced concrete mushroom column, painted white long ago and flaking, a round shaft 2 feet across flaring at the top into a wide square capital 5 feet across, 14 feet high.

A wooden shipping pallet, 4 by 4 feet, stacked with sixteen new brown corrugated cardboard record cartons in four layers, each carton about 15 by 12 by 10 inches, each marked in thick black marker "CHAIR" and a number, the top two cartons with their lids off showing file folders and clear sleeves of typed pages. About 4 and a half feet high.

A single new brown corrugated cardboard record carton, 15 by 12 by 10 inches, marked in thick black marker "CHAIR 31", its lid off and leaning against it, inside a row of file folders and a slim manila folder pulled halfway up whose tab reads exactly "C."

A single older, softer brown cardboard record carton, 15 by 12 by 10 inches, its corners rounded and slightly crushed, with a white paper label in a different, neat hand that reads exactly "EX-CORR: hold for Administrator."
An abandoned 2010s office desk in gray laminate, 5 feet wide, 2 and a half feet deep and 30 inches high, empty and dusty, with an office chair turned upside down on top of it.
A 6-foot gray plastic folding table, 30 inches deep and 29 inches high, holding a box of latex gloves, a roll of red evidence tape, a clipboard and a flashlight.
The wall of a modern federal interview room: fabric-wrapped acoustic wall panels in a dull gray-blue fine weave, each panel 4 feet wide with a thin vertical seam between panels, flat and clean.

A long one-way observation mirror set into a wall, about 8 feet wide and 3 and a half feet high, in a plain brushed aluminum frame, its surface a smooth even silvery gray mirror with no reflections shown.

A closed heavy interview room door of gray painted steel, flush, with a brushed steel lever handle on the left side and a small square wire-glass vision panel, in a gray steel frame. The vision panel glass is completely transparent.
The view through a small square door vision panel into a plain gray federal office corridor with a closed door opposite. Eye level about 5 and a half feet.
A small black security camera dome on a short white wall bracket, about 6 inches across.
A long plain interview table with a light gray laminate top and gray steel legs, 8 feet long, 3 and a half feet wide and 29 inches high, bare.
A plain gray upholstered office chair with a steel four-leg frame and armrests, about 23 inches wide and 33 inches high.
A single closed plain manila file folder lying flat, 9 by 12 inches, about a quarter inch thick, its tab blank.
A single typed letter-size page lying flat, a few paragraphs of soft unreadable text and two signatures at the bottom, a ballpoint pen beside it.
Three small plastic water bottles standing in a row beside a short stack of white paper cups, about 12 inches long in all.

styles.chr001: Bright, whimsical storybook fantasy illustration in the style of a lavishly painted modern animated Christmas film: rich, saturated color, soft rounded shapes, playful exaggerated proportions, crisp clean painted detail with gentle texture and a little magical sparkle. Santa's North Pole on Christmas Eve as a pure fantasy wonderland: candy-bright timber cottages and workshops with curly, crooked roofs piled with snow, twinkling lights, glowing lanterns, swirling green and violet aurora in a deep jewel-blue polar night sky, magical clockwork of gold and brass. A vibrant palette of cherry red, emerald and holly green, shining gold, candy pink, icy turquoise and warm candle yellow. Elves are small, round, gnome-like folk about half the height of a grown person, with big rosy button noses, round cheeks, large bright expressive eyes, long pointed ears and short sturdy limbs, wearing pointed felt caps and colorful patched wool, felt and leather with bells, buttons and stripes. Fun, warm and charming fantasy, never realistic, never gritty or dark, and no oil-painting or fine-art look. The only readable words are the ones the subject spells out, printed exactly as written and correctly spelled; all other paper and signs show soft, unreadable writing. No logos, brand names, watermarks or signatures.

looks.c001: Richly textured painterly digital art with visible brush strokes, a warm 1980s Los Angeles look.
looks.c002: Painted illustration in the manner of a 1980s paperback mystery cover and classic hand-painted point-and-click adventure game backgrounds, gouache and oil textures with visible brushwork and subtle film grain, Southern California in October 1988, a muted palette of ochre, oxblood, bottle green, slate and nicotine cream.
looks.c003: Painterly crime-drama illustration in gouache and oil with visible brushwork and a fine film grain, western Pennsylvania and Pittsburgh in October 2018, a muted industrial palette of rust, slate gray, brick red, wet asphalt and faded autumn gold.
looks.c004: Painted hard-boiled mystery illustration in gouache and oil with visible, confident brushwork, like a classic paperback mystery cover or a hand-painted adventure game background, set in Chicago in October 1927 with Art Deco, late Victorian and plain industrial detail, in a palette of amber, brass, oxblood, bottle green, slate blue and soot black.
looks.c005: In the manner of an English illuminated manuscript of the 1320s, like the Luttrell Psalter: egg tempera on vellum with crisp dark ink outlines, flat areas of color with soft modeling, fine crackle and wear in the paint, simple Gothic forms, northern England in October 1327, in ultramarine blue, vermilion, verdigris green, ochre, lead white and warm vellum cream with touches of burnished gold.
looks.c006: Contemporary painted crime-drama illustration in gouache and oil with visible brushwork and light film grain, a small former steel town on the Monongahela River in western Pennsylvania in late October 2018, in a muted palette of rust, soot brown, wet slate gray, faded brick red, olive green and autumn ochre.
looks.hallow001: Painterly gothic mystery illustration in gouache and oil with visible brushwork and fine film grain, a 1903 stone country house and its grounds in the Berkshires of rural Massachusetts in late October 2018, a restrained palette of deep oak brown, oxblood, amber, slate gray, cream and wet autumn greens.
looks.s001c01: Contemporary painted crime-drama illustration in gouache and oil with visible brushwork and fine film grain, western Pennsylvania and Pittsburgh in November 2018 with realistic 2018 objects, in a muted palette of charcoal, slate, rust and amber.
looks.s001c02: Contemporary painted crime-drama illustration in gouache and oil with visible brushwork and light film grain, set in Washington, D.C., its Maryland and Virginia suburbs and Pittsburgh in late November 2018 with realistic 2018 details, in a muted palette of charcoal, slate, rust, cream and amber.
looks.s001c03: Contemporary painted crime-drama illustration in gouache and oil with visible brushwork and light film grain, the American mid-Atlantic and western Pennsylvania in December 2018, a muted palette of charcoal, slate, rust, amber and rain-gray, realistic 2018 details.
looks.s001c04: Contemporary painted crime-drama illustration, gouache and oil with visible brushwork and light film grain, the American mid-Atlantic and western Pennsylvania in December 2018, a muted palette of charcoal, slate, rust, amber and cold gray-green, with realistic 2018 furnishings, cars and technology.
looks.s001c05: Contemporary painted crime-drama illustration, gouache and oil with visible brushwork and light film grain, Manhattan, Long Island City and downtown Pittsburgh in December 2018, in a muted palette of charcoal, slate, rust, amber and cream, with realistic 2018 furnishings, phones and screens and no 1980s styling.
looks.s001c06: Contemporary painted crime-drama illustration in gouache and oil with visible brushwork and light film grain, the American mid-Atlantic and New York City in late December 2018 with realistic 2018 objects and no 1980s styling, in a muted palette of charcoal, slate, rust, amber and cream.
looks.chr001: Bright, whimsical storybook fantasy illustration like a lavishly painted modern animated Christmas film, with rich saturated color, soft rounded shapes, playful slightly crooked proportions and crisp clean painted detail: Santa's North Pole as a magical wonderland of colorful timber, candy-bright paint, gold clockwork, holly and twinkling ornament, in a vibrant palette of cherry red, emerald green, shining gold, candy pink, icy turquoise and warm cream. Fun, warm and charming fantasy, never realistic, never gritty or dark, and no oil-painting or fine-art look.

rooms.name: Tom Hale's Bedroom
rooms.note: 418 Elm Street, a one-story 1950s stucco tract house in Mariposa Bay. Enter from the hall door in the back wall, which leads to the kitchen and hall. The bed's headboard is against the front wall.

rooms.name: Tom Hale's Kitchen
rooms.note: The kitchen and front hall of 418 Elm Street as one open room: kitchen toward the front wall, hall toward the back. Enter from the bedroom door in the back wall (left end). The right wall holds the open doorway to the garage near the front and the front door to Elm Street near the back, with the hall table between them.

rooms.name: Elm Street
rooms.note: You come out of the front door of 418 (in the back edge) and face across Elm Street toward Howard Lisk's porch. 418's front wall is the back edge of the area: its model's center is 15 feet beyond the edge, so only its facade shows, and the door piece sits on that edge over the plain panel where the model's door goes. From the back edge: 418's lawn and front walk (z 66 to 90), sidewalk (61 to 66), Elm Street curb to curb (25 to 61), the far sidewalk (20 to 25), Howard's lawn (8 to 20) and his porch, which ends at z 8; his house extends past the front edge. The corner of Elm and 3rd is off the right side.

rooms.name: Mariposa Bay Police Station
rooms.note: The detective bureau of a 1960s concrete-block police station on Harbor Boulevard. Enter from the corridor door in the back wall (right end as you come in). Windows to Harbor Boulevard in the front wall, the squad room board on the left wall, the interview room window and door on the right wall. Four steel desks in two rows with a 7-foot aisle down the middle; Ferris's is the back right one.

rooms.name: Mariposa Bay Courier
rooms.note: The newsroom of the Courier in a 1920s building at 200 Harbor Boulevard. Enter from the door in the back wall. Nora's big oak desk is front center, facing you as you walk in; four steel desks behind it in two rows with a wide center aisle. Windows to Harbor Boulevard in the front wall, the teletype on the left wall, the press room window and door on the right wall.

rooms.name: Ruth Kessler's Apartment
rooms.note: The living and dining room of a second-floor 1970s apartment near Alamitos Park, Long Beach. Enter from the apartment door in the back wall (left end). Two tall windows over the park in the front wall; the sofa against the left wall under the sisters' photograph; the dining table by the right-hand window; a closed bedroom door in the right wall.

rooms.name: Tamarack Lake General Store
rooms.note: An old knotty-pine general store at 1 Lakeshore Road, Tamarack Lake. You come in through the screen door in the back wall (which is the store's street front) and face the counter. The payphone and gas pumps are seen through that door and the wide front window beside it. The notice board and newspaper rack are on the left wall near the door; the lake window is on the right wall; the wood stove is on the right side.

rooms.name: Cabin 14
rooms.note: A clearing on the north shore road of Tamarack Lake. You arrive up the dirt road from the back and face the cabin, which stands against the front edge with its door facing you. The woodpile is to the left of the cabin, the tarped van to its right. Visit A is before the arrest (Gordon at the door, van under its tarp); visit B is after the arrest (no Gordon, the van towed, sheriff's tape where it stood).

rooms.name: Diane Moss's House
rooms.note: Diane Moss's bedroom at 1127 Sycamore Lane, Oak Terrace, a 1960s ranch house. Enter from the hall door in the back wall. The bed's headboard is against the front wall with the broken lamp on the right nightstand; the window on the right wall looks into the side yard toward the back gate; the closed door to the garage is in the left wall.

rooms.name: Blackwood Field Office
rooms.note: A small private investigator's field office on the eleventh floor of a 1920s downtown Pittsburgh office building, furnished in 2018. Enter from the building corridor through the door in the back wall; the window over the Monongahela is in the front wall behind the desk.

models.note: lab_blood
lab_gps
lab_paint
lab_gloves

rooms.name: Alder Street
rooms.note: The 400 block of Alder Street, a residential street of brick houses, on a gray, wet late-October afternoon. West is left, east is right. You arrive on the south side in front of 409 (the Marshes, back wall) and face north across the street to the oak outside 412 (front). The street runs left to right between z 16 and z 46; the road bends out of sight to the east past the Hallorans' privet at 405. Third size value is backdrop height.

rooms.name: The Marsh House
rooms.note: The open ground floor of 409 Alder Street, a 1920s brick house: the front hall and living room along the street side (back wall, where you come in), the dining table in the middle, and the kitchen along the rear of the house (front wall), with the old wall between dining room and kitchen taken out. Stairs rise along the right wall toward the kitchen. Visit A is the Marshes at home; visit B is Monday, October 29, 8:10 PM, with the front door standing open and the hall disturbed. The police state (story state C) is visit B plus officers placed in code.

rooms.name: Bellwether Police Department
rooms.note: The detective bureau on the second floor of a 1970s municipal building on Market Street. Enter from the corridor door in the back wall. Cross's desk is by the impound-lot window in the front wall; the case board is on the left wall; the door to the interview room (a separate room record, c003_police_interview) is in the right wall. The second case board (visit B) goes up once the Marshes are found.

rooms.name: Interview Room 1
rooms.note: A small interview room off the detective bureau (same location id, police). Enter from the squad room door in the back wall. Bell sits here once he is in custody.

rooms.name: Hart's Quick Stop
rooms.note: A gas station convenience store at 1820 Furnace Street. The storefront with the glass entrance doors and two big windows onto the pumps is the back wall (where you come in); the counter with the cigarette rack behind it is along the front wall, and the open door to the back office is behind the counter's right end. A side window in the left wall near the storefront looks out on the far side of the lot by the dumpster. The storefront door and both windows share one wide outside view.

rooms.name: The Kowalski House
rooms.note: The living room of Jenna's 1960s house at 27 Linden Court, where Rachel now lives with Sophie. Enter through the front door in the back wall; the kitchen opens through a wide doorway in the front wall; the window onto the backyard swing set is in the left wall; the hall desk with the envelope drawer stands against the right wall near the front door.

rooms.name: Bellwether Redevelopment Group
rooms.note: The open-plan office of Bellwether Redevelopment Group on the second floor of a renovated brick warehouse at 300 Front Street. Enter from the stair hall door in the back wall. Steel factory windows and the framed Riverside Commons rendering are on the front wall; the bookkeeper's desk with both trays is along the left wall; the credenza is against the right wall; the conference table is in the middle. Both windows share one outside view. The bank folder appears in code once E13 and E14 are found.

rooms.name: Bell Security Services
rooms.note: A two-bay steel garage at 1150 Mill Road. Enter by the steel side door in the back wall. The two roll-up bay doors and the company sign are on the front wall; Unit 4 stands nose-in in bay 2 (right) in visit A, and bay 2 is empty with an oil stain in visit B. The fleet board and workbench are on the left wall; the fridge and the open door to the small office are on the right wall. Both high windows share one outside view.

rooms.name: Shaw Towing and Recovery
rooms.note: A gravel tow yard at 4410 Route 51 on a gray, rainy late-October afternoon. You arrive at the back by the gate and face the highway fence (front). The office trailer's long side is the right edge of the yard, with wooden steps up to its door, which leads into the trailer interior (separate room record, c003_shaw_trailer). Third size value is backdrop height.

rooms.name: Shaw Towing Office Trailer
rooms.note: Inside the office trailer at the edge of the tow yard (same location id, shaw_yard). You come in through the door in the back wall, which is the long side facing the yard. A low 8-foot ceiling: it is a trailer.

rooms.name: Municipal Records Annex
rooms.note: The public reading room of the Municipal Records Annex at 14 Court Street, in a 1910s brick civic building. Enter from the vestibule door in the back wall; the sign-in counter stands near it. Tall windows onto Court Street on the front wall share one outside view. The public terminal is on the left wall; the long table with the records box and the flat-file cabinet are in the middle; the doorway in the right wall leads down to the basement archive (separate room record, c003_annex_archive), where Owen is.

rooms.name: Annex Basement Archive
rooms.note: The basement archive under the annex (same location id, annex), reached by the stairs from the reading room. You come in at the foot of the stairs through the doorway in the back wall. Rows of shelving run front to back; Owen is at the work table at the back.

rooms.name: Riverside Access Road
rooms.note: The dead end of the gravel access road off River Road, by the rail spur, on the overcast morning of Tuesday, October 30, after a night of rain. You come up the road from River Road (back) and face the river (front). The burned Unit 4 sits inside police tape by the spur; the scrapyard fence and its gate camera are back on the left, near the mouth of the road; the Bell Security site trailer and its dumpster stand across a weedy field to the right. Police tape around the trailer after the search is placed in code. Third size value is backdrop height.

rooms.name: Calder County Forensic Laboratory
rooms.note: A trace evidence lab in the county complex on Route 88, built in the 2000s, no windows. Enter by the corridor door in the back wall. The evidence lockers line the left wall; Reed's long bench with the whiteboard above it is on the right wall; fume hoods and a sink run along the front wall; an island bench stands in the middle.

rooms.name: Ashby and Lowe Detective Bureau
rooms.note: Room 714 on the seventh floor of the Haverford Building, West Monroe Street, 1927. Not the 1980s Blackwood office: designed fresh. Enter from the seventh-floor corridor through the frosted door in the back wall, near the right corner. The desk faces the door with the two windows behind it.

models.note: The invitation pushed under the door; on a rescue the same envelope lies on the desk.

rooms.name: WCRB Studio A
rooms.note: 19th floor, 412 North Michigan Avenue. 18 by 22 feet as the police photograph says (already in the bigger range). Enter through the heavy oak hall door at the left end of the back wall; the control room window is the front wall, the amplifier rack and crawlway panel are on the right (east) wall. No window to the outside. The only door is the hall door, so the locked-room puzzle holds: its 'to' is the control room by way of the hall.

decals.note: Laid flat on the carpet, head toward the control room window.

rooms.name: WCRB Control Room
rooms.note: Between Studio A and Studio B. Enter from the 19th-floor hall through the back wall. The long board runs along the front wall under the window into Studio A (curtain on the far side); the right wall has the window into Studio B; the schedule and the pen recorder are on the left wall at the board end. The floor in front of the board stays open for Samuel and Rose.

models.note: On the open shelf under the board.

rooms.name: WCRB Equipment Storage
rooms.note: At the back of the 19th floor, behind Studio A. Enter from the back hall through the door with the new lock (back wall). The crawlway panel is low in the left (west) wall, the side that backs onto Studio A. No window. The cable crates sit at the front left, clear of the panel.

models.note: The one packed too neatly on top.

rooms.name: WCRB Station Office
rooms.note: Reception and the secretary's desk, 19th floor. Enter from the corridor through the back wall door at the right. Clara's desk is on the left with the ledger shelf on the wall behind her; the glass-paneled door at the back of the right wall goes through to Victor Harlan's office (the next room record, same location).

rooms.name: Victor Harlan's Office
rooms.note: The station manager's private office, through the glass-paneled door from the station office (back wall here). Same location id as the station office; the diary is on the desk and the safe in the front right corner.

rooms.name: WCRB Recording Workshop
rooms.note: Where the station cuts its own discs, 19th floor. Enter from the hall through the back wall door at the right. The disc rack stands against the left wall, the bench with the lathe in the middle of the room, the playback turntable on the right. One window on the front wall, the same Michigan Avenue view as the station office.

rooms.name: The Blue Lantern
rooms.note: Behind Lantern Cigars, 818 North Clark Street. Enter from the cigar store stockroom through the back wall door. The long bar runs down the left wall with the crates behind it; the bandstand with the piano is against the front wall under the blue lantern; the back office door is near the back of the right wall. No windows. The framed photograph is on the wall beside the piano (a wall piece, with a matching small standing frame on the piano as a model to use if Ian prefers it on the piano top).

rooms.name: Russo's Back Office
rooms.note: The small office off the Blue Lantern's floor, through the door in the right wall of the club (back wall here). Same location id as the club; the desk with the spike holds Russo's payment note (E23).

rooms.name: Henry Mercer's Apartment
rooms.note: 1140 North Dearborn Street, Apartment 3B, a one-room bachelor apartment shut up since the landlord padlocked it on Oct. 15. Enter through the hall door at the left end of the back wall; the landlord's notice is tacked to the inside of that door. The rolltop desk is by the front window, the mantel with the bills on the left wall, the furniture under dust sheets.

models.note: On the writing surface in front of the closed tambour.

rooms.name: Louise Vale's Parlor
rooms.note: 5418 Dorchester Avenue, Hyde Park, a 1900s greystone. Enter from the front hall through the wide cased opening in the back wall. The piano stands against the right wall with the photograph on top and the letter on its music desk; the mirror draped in crepe hangs on the left wall over the sofa; two lace-curtained windows look onto Dorchester Avenue in the front wall.

models.note: Propped on the music desk.

rooms.name: Chicago Police Detective Bureau
rooms.note: The squad room at headquarters on South State Street. Enter from the corridor through the back wall door; a clear aisle runs up the middle to the blackboard on the front wall, with three desks each side. The tall windows on the left wall look onto State Street; the holding cell door is near the back of the right wall, where Victor Harlan is held after his arrest.

rooms.name: Doyle's Rooms
rooms.note: 2214 South Halsted Street. One open space for the front hall and parlor: enter by the front door at the left end of the back wall; the front desk with the register and the key board are on the left, the staircase climbs along the left wall toward the front; the parlor side on the right has the card table, the radio and the settee, with two windows onto Halsted Street in the front wall.

rooms.name: Riverside Shipping and Storage
rooms.note: 640 West Kinzie Street. The yard and the night gate (wh_night_gate) are the same place, so one room: visit A is warehouse_gate on a gray October afternoon; visit B is wh_night_gate on Monday night, Oct. 24. You come in through the gate on Kinzie Street (back) and face the river (front). The long warehouse runs down the right side; its last three river doors, bays 4 to 6, stand at the river end where the yard meets the pier, with bay 6 nearest the water. On visit B the doors are chained.

models.note: On the bay 6 hasp; Frankie lets it down when he unchains the door.
The car whose headlights swing in at the gate (E27).

rooms.name: A Dark Storeroom
rooms.note: Upstairs at Riverside Shipping, at the river end, Monday night. The boarded window in the front wall faces the river and the Wells Street bridge; the plank door to the stairs (where Sal and Augie talk) is in the back wall; the inner door to the tally office is in the right wall, fastened on this side with the hasp and padlock (a separate piece, so code can take it off).

rooms.name: The Tally Office
rooms.note: Next to the storeroom, upstairs at the river end, above bay 6. Come in from the storeroom through the inner door in the left wall (it lines up with the storeroom's right-wall door). The window over the river is in the front wall, the hand lamp on its hook beside it; the open stair head down to bay 6 is in the right wall, with the stenciled crate in front of it.

rooms.name: Bay 6, the River Door
rooms.note: Ground floor of Riverside Shipping, bay 6, under the tally office. You come down the stair into the left wall near the back; the barred river door is in the front wall and swings out over the pier. Its outside view is the pier, the bridge stairs to the left and the gate lamp up the yard to the right (the views for a3_gate_seen and a3_riverpath). On a rescue the others wait on the pier with Frankie (outside, not in the room).

models.note: Across the door in its brackets, about 4 feet up; lifted out in code.

rooms.name: The Wells Street Bridge
rooms.note: The sidewalk on the lower deck of the Wells Street bridge, Monday night, Oct. 24, 1927, a long strip (60 by 16 feet) along the rail. Face the front to look across the river at the back of Riverside Shipping; the tally office window (the dark glass one beside the boarded one) is where the six-flash signal shows, done in code. The iron stairs to the riverbank are at the right (north) end.

rooms.name: Your Chamber
rooms.note: An upper chamber in the abbey guest-house on the west side of the outer court; enter by the oak door in the back wall. The window in the front wall looks over the outer court to the gatehouse and bell tower.

rooms.name: The Book Room
rooms.note: A small vaulted stone room off the cloister's west walk; enter from the walk through the forced doorway at the left end of the back wall. The desk stands under the window in the front wall, the charter chest against the right wall, the stool between them, as in Thomas's sketch. The door bar's bracket is in the corner beside the doorway and the candle aumbry is just round the corner on the left wall; the cellarer's passage runs on the other side of the left wall.

rooms.name: The Cloister
rooms.note: The cloister's west walk, a roofed stone walk 12 feet wide; you come along it from the south walk (the back arch) and face north toward the corner where the north walk (the scriptorium) turns east. The left wall holds the cellarer's passage door and, about 8 feet further on, the book room doorway; the right wall is the open arcade onto the garth, with the chapter house door seen across it.

rooms.name: The Scriptorium
rooms.note: The carrels along the cloister's north walk, against the church's south wall. You face south across the garth through four window bays, each with a carrel; Edmund's is the first on the left. The west walk (the cloister) opens through the arch in the right wall; the processional door into the church is in the back wall near its left end.

rooms.name: The Abbey Church
rooms.note: The choir of the abbey church: you come in through the doorway in the choir screen (back wall) and face east to the high altar under the east window. The two rows of stalls face each other down the middle. The sacristy door and its inventory board are on the left (north) wall near the altar; the Lady altar stands against the right (south) wall under the painted Virgin, with the processional door to the cloister further back on that wall.

rooms.name: The Abbot's Chamber
rooms.note: An upper chamber above the outer parlor, reached by a stair; enter by the door at the left end of the back wall. The hooded fireplace with the carved saint on its mantel is on the left wall, the table with the account roll in the middle, the side table with the letters against the right wall, the window in the front wall.

rooms.name: The Cellarer's Passage
rooms.note: A narrow vaulted passage running west from the cloister's west walk (door in the back wall) to the kitchen court (door in the front wall), along the south side of the book room. The aumbry's back door, its rough frame and the cellar hook are on the right wall near the cloister end, opposite the book room's aumbry; the stores line the left wall.

rooms.name: The Cellar and the Checker
rooms.note: The vaulted cellar of the cellarer's range, entered from the kitchen court through the wide doorway in the back wall. Two timber partitions make two bays at the front: the checker (the cellarer's office) on the left, with the habit on its peg, the desk, day book and tally box, and the salt store on the right, with the salt bin and casks of salt fish. Ale casks line the right wall.

rooms.name: The Kitchen Court
rooms.note: The small cobbled court west of the cloister range, open to the rain. The cellar's wide doorway (with the court lamp over it) is on the back side, the guest-house kitchen's door and window face it across the court, the passage door is in the corner at the back end of the left side, and an archway on the right side leads to the outer court.

rooms.name: The Gatehouse
rooms.note: The vaulted gate passage: you come in from the outer court through the inner arch (back wall) and face the barred great gate (front wall). The porter's lodge door, its shuttered window and the gate roll on its board are on the left wall; the porter's bench is against the right wall.

rooms.name: The Mill at Hollin Bridge
rooms.note: Inside the small stone mill: enter by the open door in the back wall from the yard and the bridge. The wheel turns just outside the big opening in the right wall, driving the millstones beside it; the loft platform and its ladder stand in the front left corner.

rooms.name: Ashcombe Hall
rooms.note: The great hall of Lord Roland's manor: you come in through the screen at the low end (back wall) and face the dais and high table at the far end, under the painted cloth and the Ashcombe arms. The open hearth is in the middle of the floor with the hound beside it; trestle tables line both sides; the open door to the yard is near the back of the right wall.

rooms.name: The Muniment Room Door
rooms.note: The small stone landing at the top of the stair above the chapter house, in front of the triple-locked door. Until RE08 this is all of the muniment room you can reach; after RE08 the door in the front wall opens into the room.

rooms.name: The Muniment Room
rooms.note: The locked record room above the chapter house, open only after RE08: enter through the triple-locked door in the back wall. The seal cabinet with the chronicle on it is on the left wall, the necrology on its stand and the table in the middle, the iron-bound chests along the right wall, a narrow window in the front wall over the cloister.

rooms.name: The Infirmary
rooms.note: The long infirmary hall east of the cloister; enter by the door at the left end of the back wall. Brother Edmund lies on his bier along the left side between two candle stands; Brother Odo's bed is against the right wall; the small fireplace is in the front wall; the windows on the left wall look onto the herb garden.

rooms.name: The Bell Tower
rooms.note: The bell chamber high in the tower over the crossing, entered by the low door in the back wall from the tower stair. The great bell hangs in its oak frame in the middle, the new rope hanging from its wheel and the old one coiled on the floor beside it; louvered openings high in the front, left and right walls; the chained customary and the ringer's chalk board on the left wall.

rooms.name: Blackwood Field Office
rooms.note: The front room of two rented rooms above Kovar Hardware on Second Street, in an 1890s brick building. You come up the stairs and in through the half-glass door in the back wall; the two street windows are in the front wall. Visit B: the black pickup idles across the street.

rooms.name: Hollow Creek Steel: East Gate
rooms.note: The gravel shoulder of Mill Road at the East Gate. You arrive from the road (back); the fence and gate are the front edge, the north fence with the break runs along the right edge. Visit B (Chapter 6): the gate stands open and a police SUV is parked on the shoulder.

rooms.name: East Mill Shop Floor
rooms.note: Ground floor of the two-story brick East Mill Maintenance Building. You come in through the open freight doorway in the back wall from the East Gate side. Tool Crib 4 is a mesh cage built against the front brick wall (x 17 to 27, z 0 to 12) with its door in its left face, straight across from the workbench on the left wall: 14 feet from the bench's front edge to the crib door. The steel loft runs along the left wall behind the bench. Visit A is the shop as first found; visit B is the Chapter 6 reconstruction (location mill_reconstruction): work lights, tape, shoring and the copper in the loft.

rooms.name: Tool Crib 4
rooms.note: The inside of the mesh cage on the shop floor. You come in through the cage door in the back wall. The left wall is the building's brick wall (the shop's front wall); the other three walls and the roof are mesh. Kept at its true 10 by 12 feet because the police sketch (E013) and the story give that size. The mesh wall and ceiling could later become cutout walls so the shop shows through.

rooms.name: West End Administration Building
rooms.note: The general manager's old corner office on the top floor of the four-story administration building, abandoned since 2003. You come in from the hall door in the back wall; the big window in the front wall looks out over the West End. The four records cartons sit in a row on the floor in front of the desk.

rooms.name: Former Maintenance Office
rooms.note: The maintenance director's office, a block-walled room on the ground floor behind No. 2 Reheat in the West End. You come in from the steel door in the back wall. The pipes run along the ceiling near the left wall.

rooms.name: West End Loading Yard
rooms.note: The yard behind No. 2 Reheat. You arrive from the administration building side (back) and face the furnace building. The Gallery B hatch is in the middle of the yard, beside the rail track that runs from front to back along the left side; the climb down is a hotspot action (E030 is its evidence picture), not a walkable room.

rooms.name: Former Mill Medical Station
rooms.note: The plant's first-aid room in a small brick building by the West End main gate. You come in through the door in the back wall; the window in the front wall looks out at the gate.

rooms.name: West End Gate and River Ramp
rooms.note: Just inside the West End main gate. You arrive from the entrance road (back) and face the river; the boat ramp runs down to the river at the front edge. Trent Protective's trailer is on the left, the old guardhouse in the middle by the gate. The clipboard inside the trailer and the logs inside the guardhouse are hotspots on those models.

rooms.name: Abandoned Rail Service Building
rooms.note: A tall brick rail service building that Mon Valley Scrap used as its weigh house. You come in through the open freight doorway in the back wall. The weigh office booth stands against the right wall with its counter and window facing the platform scale in the middle of the floor. The painted sign is on the left wall.

rooms.name: Lasko House: Emily's Room
rooms.note: Emily's upstairs bedroom at 418 Fourth Street, kept as it was in 1996. You come in from the upstairs hall door in the back wall. The bed's headboard is against the left wall with the box of her things on it; the calendar hangs on the left wall above the bed and the family photographs on the right wall. Sarah stands in the open middle of the room.

rooms.name: Reeves Auto Repair
rooms.note: A two-bay block garage at 77 Water Street. You come in through the customer door in the back wall; the two overhead doors are in the front wall with the lift behind the left one. The counter and register run along the right wall with the work order rack and Gus's photo above it. The wooden loft runs along the back half of the left wall, reached by the open stair; the invoice books and parts ledgers are up on the loft (they sit at loft height, onFt 9). The welder shelf is under the loft.

rooms.name: Hollow Creek Police Department
rooms.note: The detectives' room on the second floor of the 1930s Borough Building on Market Street. You come in from the hall door in the back wall. The long table with the 1996 case box and folders is by the front-left window; Mitchell's corkboard and the interview room door are on the right wall. The board changes after Glenn's death (visit B).

models.hotspot: pd_report, pd_notes, pd_inventory, pd_wade96, pd_rebecca96, pd_andrew96

rooms.name: Hollow Creek Police: Interview Room
rooms.note: Split out of the police location: the interview room off the detectives' room, where Michael Trent sits after his arrest (pd_trent). You come in through the steel door in the back wall; the observation mirror is on the left wall.

rooms.name: County Forensic Office
rooms.note: The medical examiner's anthropology lab in a county building on Greensburg Pike. You come in from the corridor door in the back wall. The light box is on the left wall, the covered exam table in the right half of the room, the lab counter along the right wall.

rooms.name: The Mon Valley Record
rooms.note: The ground-floor newsroom in a 1900s Main Street storefront. You come in from the back hall door; the two big front windows look out on Main Street. The directory shelf stands at the left wall near the front window; the bound volumes are on the right wall. Jessica's desk, with the box of her old tapes, is the back-right desk.

rooms.name: Borough Municipal Records
rooms.note: The records room in the Borough Building basement. You come in from the stair door in the back wall. A row of filing cabinets runs along the left wall, shelving along the right; the long table in the middle holds the open Riverside Works file and the index card box.

rooms.name: County Regulatory Archive
rooms.note: A second-floor archive room in the county annex on Courthouse Square. You come in from the corridor door in the back wall. Rows of archive shelving fill the left half; the cart of OSHA boxes and the worktable with the fire marshal's file and the interview binder are near the front window.

rooms.name: County Courthouse Records
rooms.note: The Recorder of Deeds office on the courthouse ground floor. You come in through the hall door in the back wall and stand on the public side of the long counter, which crosses the room 16 feet from the front wall. Behind the counter, the deed book shelves line the left wall to near the ceiling, and Karen works there.

rooms.name: Steelworkers Local 2177 Hall
rooms.note: The meeting hall of the local on Seventh Street. You come in through the double doors in the back wall. The bar runs along the front wall under the local's banner; the card tables fill the middle; the grievance cabinet stands at the left wall near the front, and the memorial wall and the television are on the right wall. Earl and Ray sit at the card tables.

rooms.name: Sutter House: Den
rooms.note: The front room of a small 1950s brick house at 31 Orchard Lane. You come in through the front door in the back wall. Glenn's desk is in the front-left corner, his bass, wedding photo and plaque on the left wall; doorways in the right wall lead to the kitchen (nearer the front) and the bedroom. Glenn is here on visit A only. On the sealed state (sutter_home B) the walk should stop at the front walk room.

rooms.name: Sutter House: Kitchen
rooms.note: Through the den's front doorway. You come in through the doorway in the back wall. The refrigerator with Glenn's calendar stands at the right wall.

rooms.name: Sutter House: Bedroom
rooms.note: Through the den's back doorway. You come in through the doorway in the back wall. The bed's headboard is against the front wall with the nightstand and Bible on its right side.

rooms.name: Sutter House: Front Walk
rooms.note: Added so the sealed state (sutter_home B) has a place to stand: the front yard of 31 Orchard Lane. You arrive from the street (back) and face the house. The police tape covers the front door on visit B only; on the other visits the door opens into the den.

rooms.name: Creekside Self Storage: Unit 14
rooms.note: Glenn's 10 by 20 foot unit widened to 12 by 24. You come in under the raised roll-up door in the back wall, so the oil spill with marker 6 and the photo board are just inside it. The office is a separate building across the aisle (the next room); walking out of the unit and back in through the office door connects them.

rooms.name: Creekside Self Storage: Office
rooms.note: Split out of the storage location: the facility office where the manager prints the gate report (cs_log) and keeps the contracts (cs_contract). You come in through the glass door in the back wall, the window in the front wall looks out at the keypad gate.

rooms.name: Stroud Riverfront Development
rooms.note: The restored lobby of the old bank at Main and Second, now Stroud's reception. You come in through the bronze doors in the back wall; the tall arched windows are in the front wall. The framed grant letter and the rendering hang side by side on the right wall (the letter's evidence text says it is beside the rendering), and the old vault door is a showpiece on the left wall. Stroud receives you by the sitting area.

rooms.name: Trent Protective Services
rooms.note: A one-room office in a cinderblock building at 400 Railroad Street, paneled inside. You come in through the steel door in the back wall; the window in the front wall looks onto the gravel lot and the tracks. Visit B is after the State Police search (trent_office B): the notice on the inside of the door, the desk emptied and the computer gone. The green ledger is on the desk in both visits.

rooms.name: Greer House: Front Porch
rooms.note: Added for Len's porch (gh_porch) and the Kovach door (gh_neighbor): the front yard of 6 Hilltop Road. You arrive from the road (back) and face the porch. The Kovach front door stands at the right edge of the yard, in front of the backdrop of her house next door. Len is here on visit A; on visit B (missing person scene) the front door leads into the hall.

rooms.name: Greer House: Front Hall
rooms.note: The front hall of the ranch. You come in through the front door in the back wall; the wide opening in the front wall leads to the kitchen and dining room. Visit B is the missing person scene: rug shoved, photo crooked, glasses on the floor by the coat rack. The living room door on the left wall stays shut.

rooms.name: Greer House: Kitchen and Dining Room
rooms.note: An eat-in kitchen with the dining table, through the hall's wide opening (back wall). The counter with the coffee maker and the pill organizers is on the right wall under the coffee can shelf; the dining table with the lawyer's letter is in the middle. Visit B adds the pills, the untouched supper, the letter and the fork on the floor.

rooms.name: Laurel Hollow Road
rooms.note: A stretch of dirt road in the ridges before dawn. You arrive from below (back), with the two State Police cruisers parked behind you; the pipe gate crosses the road ahead. Once Trent is arrested, walking through the gate leads up the road to the camp (lr_up).

rooms.name: The Camp
rooms.note: The main room of the Trents' two-room cabin, with the kitchen end at the front. You come in through the plank door in the back wall (antlers above it). The wood stove stands at the left wall under the shelf with the coffee can; the trap door to the cellar is open in the kitchen end of the floor (the floor needs a 3-foot square hole there); the door in the right wall to the bunk room stays shut. The cellar itself is evidence only (E072). No ceiling fixture: the cabin has no power.

rooms.name: Corso Photo and Frame
rooms.note: The front shop at 211 Main Street. You come in from the street door in the back wall (the shop window is beside it); the curtained doorway in the front wall leads to the back room with the cabinet and the darkroom.

rooms.name: Corso Photo and Frame: Back Room
rooms.note: Split out of the corso_photo location: the back room through the curtained doorway. You come in through that doorway in the back wall. Vince's oak filing cabinet stands at the left wall; the darkroom door, with its red safelight above, is in the front wall and stays shut (cf_darkroom is a look, not a room); the shop's back door to the alley is in the right wall.

rooms.name: Sloan House
rooms.note: Rebecca's kitchen at 22 Larch Street. You come in from the living room door in the back wall. The refrigerator with the prom photo stands at the right wall; the round table is in the middle.

rooms.name: Pierce House
rooms.note: The basement rec room at 9 Pike Alley, where Andrew talks and sets his mother's shoebox on the card table. You come in from the stair door in the back wall. The furnace is in the front-right corner; the shelves of shoeboxes stand along the right wall.

rooms.name: The Morning Room
rooms.note: A paneled main-floor room at the front of the 1903 house, given to Blackwood as an incident room. Enter from the entrance hall door in the back wall; the tall window in the front wall looks down the drive to the gatehouse.

rooms.name: Entrance Hall
rooms.note: The high stone hall at the center of the main floor. The front door is in the front wall; the main stair rises along the right wall to a half-landing and turns up through an arch to the upstairs corridor. Doors on the left wall lead to the morning room and the dining room; doors in the back wall lead to the library and the conservatory.

rooms.name: Grand Dining Room
rooms.note: A long formal dining room on the main floor. Enter from the entrance hall through the double doors in the back wall. The table runs front to back with the head (Ambrose's chair) toward the windows and the thirteenth place at the foot near the doors. Three tall windows in the front wall look down the drive to the gate.

rooms.name: The Library
rooms.note: A tall book-lined room on the main floor, the Blackthorn Foundation's archive. Enter from the entrance hall through the double doors in the back wall. Bookcases line the side walls; the narrow service door in the paneling near the front of the right wall goes down to the service corridor.

rooms.name: The Conservatory
rooms.note: A Victorian glass room off the back of the entrance hall: a red brick knee wall with tall white-framed glazing above on three sides and a glass roof. Enter from the house door in the back wall; the glazed garden door in the middle of the front wall opens onto the terrace.
